speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

I wish to call the attention of the Prime Minister, who is also Acting Minister of Militia, to a case that has been placed before me by the Rev. J.
O.	Dube, parish priest of iSt. Godefroy, in the county of Bonaventure, relating to Private Adolphe Grenier No. 416278, of the 24th, formerly 41st Overseas Battalion. This is rather an unusual case. This young man, 20 years of age, enlisted in Hull
on February 18, 1915, and was reported on the 13th of March last as having been " killed in action March 3rd." On attestation the name and address of the next of kin were not stated. He was the adopted son of Pierre LeCourtois and his wife, Genevieve Roussy. These people took him when he was two months old, and brought him up until he was 20 years of age. Last year he happened to be in Hull working for a lumber firm, and he enlisted there and went to the front. He gave on enlistment the name of Adolphe Grenier, presuming that this was the name of his father, although he had been brought up by these two persons whom I have mentioned, who are very humble fishing folks. The question now arises who will succeed to whatever balance of pay has been left by him, and an insurance policy of $1,000 which he has referred to in two scraps of letters which I have in my hand. One of these is written in lead pencil and in it he says he is taking out an insurance policy on behalf of his adopted mother. There is a second letter, dated 12 August, 1915, in which he bids her a fond farewell on the eve of going into action, and hopes he will be able to get through all right, but if he does not he leaves everything to her. It is rather a pathetic letter, and looks as if he had a premonition of his fate. He refers to the sacrifice he is about to make for his Mother Country, England and Canada, and for all the citizens of this country. In addition to this, there is a letter, which I think worth reading, from the commanding Dfiicer of the corps to which this young man belonged:
Flanders, 19/3/16.
Dear Mr. Grenier :
Ere this letter reaches you, you will no doubt have heard from the department at Ottawa of the death of your son.
As his Commanding Officer I desire to place on record my appreciation of the faithful and efficient services which he has rendered and which has been an inspiration to all ranks
I count it a great honour to have in my battalion quite a number of French Canadian soldiers, and they have all been looked upon by my officers and myself as the mainstay of the section to which they belong.
If at any time I can be of service to you, please write me, and if spared, I shall be only too glad to do anything I can to show my deep appreciation of the good work done by your son.
On behalf of my officers, N.C.O.'s and men, I extend our heartfelt sympathy.
Believe me,
Yours sincerely,
J. H. Gunn, Lt.-Col.

From this correspondence, which the reverend gentleman has sent .to me, I see that the officer in charge of the estates of deceased soldiers says that it may take about four or five months before the department will be in a position to deal with the case. The reverend gentleman calls attention to the unusual circumstances that no kin are referred to in the attestation. He was the adopted son of these people; and by these letters, which evidently are a .testament, whatever legal value they may have, he has left all that belonged to him to hie adopted mother, Mrs. Pierre Le-Courtois.

I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce a matter which I deem important.
I have here a letter dated Oporto, 19th April, 1916. I need not read the whole letter. The concluding paragraph is as follows:
Owing to the high prices to which food has risen in this country, due in great measure to the low exchange, the Government recently appointed Food Commissioners to study the question. Yesterday a law came into force fixing arbitrary maximum prices for codfish considerably below the prices at which we have been selling, these being already below what shippers require for their fish. The law mentions codfish but does not specify the origin. We are therefore in doubt as to whether it applies to imported fish or only to the Portuguese cure. In the meantime we have closed all our stores and have applied to the Civil Governor for a definition of the codfish coming within the decree. We have also made representations of our case to the British minister at Lisbon.

1.	Has the Provincial Act, passed by the Legislature of British Columbia obliging Joint Stock Companies operating under letters patent granted by the Federal Government to register in British Columbia and pay a license fee to the Government of that province in order to do business there, been declared ultra vires by a judgment of the Privy Council?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN AND GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAYS.

speechtext:
Sir THOMAS WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I avail myself of the opportunity afforded by this motion to make a statement respecting the proposed loans of $8,000,000 to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and $15,000,000 to the Canadian Northern Railway, which are contained in the Supplementary Estimates recently presented to the House, and also respecting the policy of the Government regarding the general railway situation of Canada. The loans in question are, in the view of the Government, necessitated from considerations of public interest by Teason of the critical position of the financial affairs of these two companies. The House will recall that two years ago legislation was passed by Parliament under which, hy a. guarantee of securities, aid was afforded to the two companies for the purpose of the completion of their enterprises. It was the view at that time that the proceeds of the securities so guaranteed, amounting to $45,000,000 in the case of the Canadian Northern and $16,000,000 in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific would be sufficient for the purposes which were had
in view. Within .a few weeks after the legislation had been passed, and almost immediately after the completion and execution of the two trust deeds securing the issues of securities to which I have referred, war broke out. The immediate effect of the war, and its indirect result upon business and finance, was to close the London market, -and indeed the markets of the world, to the issue of further securities except those of governments for the purpose of the prosecution o*f the war. In order that the intention of Parliament, as evidenced by the legislation to which I have referred, might be carried out, and the work upon these two Transcontinental railway systems continued, the Dominion Government made loans in Dominion notes upon a portion of Ithe guaranteed securities. The amount advanced to the Canadian Northern Railway Company was $10,000,000, and the amount advanced to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company was $6,000,000. In the case of the Canadian Northern loan of $10,000,000 security was taken to the amount of $12,500,000 of its guaranteed securities, and in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific, railway security was taken to the amount of $7,500,000 of its guaranteed securities. These loans were made and the transactions in question were subsequently ratified by Parliament. It was felt at the time that it was in the national interest that these two undertakings upon which so much public money had been expended, should be pushed to completion.
I may say that when war broke out it was the expectation of many that a few months would witness its termination, and it was hoped that the dislocation of business, and the derangement of world finance which ensued upon its outbreak, would consequently be of only temporary duration. These hopes and expectations havp been disappointed, the war having increased in magnitude and intensity since its outbreak with no prospect, so far as one can see at the present time, of its early conclusion; indeed, all the indications seem to point rather to an indefinite prolongation of the great struggle in which we are engaged.
The war has affected the two great railway companies in question in two ways; in the first place they were both obliged to dispose of their securities, including the guaranteed securities which I have mentioned, at	a lower price	than
they would have been able to realize had the war not broken put. There has been a material shrinkage in the case of guaranteed securities. It will

be recalled by the House that, in addition to the $45,000,000 of guaranteed securities, the Canadian Northern Railway Company had some $55,000,000 of further securities, which were to be marketed and the proceeds devoted to the completion of its enterprise. As market conditions have been, the Canadian Northern Railway Company has not been able to realize within $10,500,000 of the amount which it expected to realize under the prices which prevailed prior to the outbreak of the war. The first year of the war, by reason of the interruption to general business, saw a great falling off in the earnings of all the railway systems of Canada. In the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the premier railway system of the Dominion, there was a drop in gross earnings from $130,000,000 to $99,000,000, a reduction of about 25 per cent. In the case of the net earnings of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, there was a drop of about the same percentage, from $42,000,000 to $33,000,000. On account of the abundant crop, particularly in the West, railway earnings during the past year have been considerably improved, but in this connection it is to be borne in mind that we had, particularly in the Western part of Canada, a winter1, of unusual severity, and the operating expenses of all railways have in consequence been .greatly increased over the ordinary. As a result of these conditions the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have been unable to market their securities at the prices Which they expected to realize at the time the legislation guaranteeing the issue of $45,000,000 and $16,000,000 respectively was passed. There was also* as I stated, a reduction in earnings for the first year after the outbreak of the war over what they might have hoped to obtain had peace conditions prevailed. In addition, by reason of the difficulties of finance brought about by the war, there was delay in completion of the work which the two railway companies had in view. In the case of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, the through service was linked up only last December, a delay of nearly a year over the period which that company had in view previous to the outbreak of the war.
In these conditions the affairs of these two railway companies, which have been so largely aided by the public credit, have given the Government considerable anxiety for many months past. With improving

financial conditions and with better earnings in prospect, .it was hoped that no material assistance would be required in addition to the aid which was given in 1914; but it is now clear, from the statements presented by the railway companies in question, which statements I have laid upon the table of the House, from the financial conditions which still prevail, and from the fact that the war is still raging, that relief is absolutely necessary if these two railway companies are to continue as solvent going concerns. It has been the policy of the Government since the outbreak of the war to maintain stability and to promote confidence in the financial and economic situation of Canada. We have, therefore, as I have stated, looked with growing concern upon the financial position of these two great transcontinental enterprises whose affairs have become so intimately connected with the public credit both of the Dominion and of the provinces of Canada. Securities to the amount of several hundred millions of dollars have been issued by both these companies and have found their way into the hands of investors in Great Britain, the United States, and Europe. Any financial crisis in their affairs could not but react seriously upon the general credit of the Dominion in the eyes of the outside world.
Without further elaborating these points, which are, I think, sufficiently within the knowledge of the House, I desire to refer briefly to the present financial position of these two railway companies. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company is now completed from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert. That company has issued securities guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada to the amount, in round figures, of $78,000,000. Jn addition, loans have been made by the Dominion Government, under this and the preceding Administration, to an amount of $25,000,000, making a total of Dominion guarantees and Dominion loans of an amount exceeding $100,000,000. In addition, the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta have given their guarantees in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company, which is a subsidiary of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, to the amount of $13,000,000; so that, in round figures, the position, so far as the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company is concerned, is that it has outstanding securities guaranteed by the Dominion Government to the extent of $78,000,000; it has obtained loans from the Dominion Government to the amount of $25,000,000, and the Grand Trunk

Pacific Branch Lines Company has issued securities to the amount of $13,000,000, guaranteed by the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Therefore in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, the public credit of the Dominion and of the two provinces in question is involved to the extent of no less a sum than $115,000,000. In addition to the guarantees which have been given by the Dominion Government and by the Provincial Governments of 'Saskatchewan and Alberta upon the securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and its subsidiary companies, the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada has guaranteed additional securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to a total amount of $97,000,000.
The House is, no doubt, aware that it has been by the conjunction of the credit of the Dominion Government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company has been enabled to pursue its enterprise to completion. In addition to the $97,000,000 to which I have already referred as guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, that company has made advances to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, to the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company and to the Grand Trunk Pacific Development Company, the latter being also a subsidiary company of the Grand Trunk Pacific, an amount exceeding $25,000,000, for which it holds the notes of the companies in question, and a comparatively small amount, I think $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 of the securities of the Grand Trunk Branch Lines Company which, as I stated, are guaranteed by the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. The Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada is, of course, a powerful corporation. But in common with all other companies, it has experienced and is still experiencing the adverse financial conditions produced by the war. It finds itself now, from considerations affecting its credit, unable to extend further aid to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company whose securities it has guaranteed to the amount I have stated and to which and its subsidiary companies it has made these advances exceeding $25,000,000. This is all the more the case because of the virtual closing of the London market to all new issues. In addition, the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada finds itself confronted with the necessity of providing for
betterments, improvements and terminal facilities involving the expenditure of large sums of money, upon its own system throughout Canada. I have stated that from considerations affecting its credit the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada finds itself unable to extend further aid to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company or its subsidiaries; and in that connection I desire to read extracts from the letters of Mr. Alfred W. Smithers, chairman of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, which are published in the financial statements relating to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company which I laid upon the Table, and copies of which have been distributed to members of the House. Mr. Smithers says:	[DOT]
Under present circumstances it is quite impossible for the Grand Trunk Railway Company to meet the extra liabilities arising from the Grand Trunk Pacific railway.
And further:
We have done our utmost to meet the heavy financing which has been necessary, and the difficulty of which has been immensely increased by the disastrous war conditions. We are now " at the end of our tether " with regard to Grand Trunk Pacific financing.
The first Grand Trunk Pacific payments for interest after the 1st January next will become due on the 1st March, and amount to just under $1,000,000, and there is no prospect of our being able to meet that payment.
And he goes on to say:
The railway situation in Canada is a serious one, and any default on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company might lead to grave consequences as to the general financial position in Canada. The Board believe this danger will pass away if the Government accept their proposal, thus saving the general situation, and enabling the Grand Trunk Railway Company, as I have already explained, to fulfil its duty to the public.
From the figures I have given and the statements I have made it will be seen that the credit and standing of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada are vitally bound up with the condition confronting the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. The Grand Trunk Pacific railway is now out of the construction stage. I desire to say a word concerning its financial position. Its fixed charges for the present year amount to $7,200,000, representing, of course, the interest upon its securities. To this must be added a deficit on operating account and for maintenance and exceptional repairs of $2,000,000, making a total exceeding $9,000,000 of a deficit expected upon the operations of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for

the coming year. In addition, I should state to the House that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada are in arrears of interest payments to the Dominion Government upon the loan of $25,000,000 made to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company hy the Government. The amount of such arrears on the 1st of April last was $1,350,000. I have laid upon the table of the House a statement, signed t>v the VicePresident and Treasurer of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, showing the details of the totals which I have mentioned. In a word, the position is this: Expected deficit upon operation and fixed charges for the coming year, $9,000,000; arrears of interest 'to the Dominion Government, $1,350,000.

speechtext: Is it my hon. friend's opinion that, war or no war, he will have to take over at least one of the two railways?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN AND GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I am afraid I am taking up too long a time, but I -regard the subject as one of considerable importance. I will come to that point in a moment or

two. The first business of Canada at the present time is the war; all other businesses, no matter how important they may be, are subsidiary and subordinate. What I am trying to show the House is this, that in the midst of the war, to undertake its burdens and at the same time to undertake the financing of two transcontinental railway systems would be a formidable proposition even for the Dominion Government.
The third alternative, and the one which we now propose to Parliament, is to afford the minimum of temporary assistance which will enable these two systems to continue in operation pending an investigation, which we propose to carry out by the best experts available, into the fiscal, economic and financial conditions of the railway situation as it exists in Canada to-day. It is perfectly clear that it is not possible, nor in the national interest, that we should go on, as has been the case for many years past under this and the preceding Government, making loans or giving guarantees at short intervals for the purpose of assisting these two large enterprises. A continuing condition such as this would be intolerable, and the time has arrived when, in our judgment, it has become imperatively necessary that a permanent solution should be found for the existing railway situation. No doubt that situation has been aggravated by the war, but it is none the less necessary that some permanent policy should be adopted. We cannot adopt a permanent policy until we know all the facts and have been advised by those most capabie of giving advice as to what is really involved in the problem which confronts us and what the future of the existing systems is likely to be. We cannot adopt such a policy until we know what, if any, rearrangement, redistribution or linking up of existing lines or systems, may be necessary in order to get the best economic result from the enormous expenditures which have been made upon Canada's railway systems. It is possible, and even probable, that the permanent solution of this great question may involve the Dominion taking over one or more of the existing systems, or there may be involved the larger issue of nationalization of all the railways of Canada. The whole question is so vast in its complexity and manifold in its bearings that nothing but a thorough mastery of the problems involved, upon the best information and advice obtainable, can lead to its proper solution. Nevertheless, for reasons which
I have given, this problem must now be faced, and the present measure of aid is designed as a temporary expedient to meet the situation as it is until such time as the whole problem can he fully studied and solved.
The House will observe that the loans which we propose, of $15,000,000 and $8,000,000 respectively, are repayable upon demand, so that, in a sense, we have a control of the situation through those demand loans. We are charging a rate of interest of six per cent, the Dominion Government being able to borrow at slightly less than that figure. We realize that the security upon which we are making these loans to both of the railway systems in question is rather slender, and therefore we have a vital interest in the administration of the affairs of these two railways. It is our intention, in order that we may be kept fully informed, pending our investigation by experts, which I have announced, as to the condition and administration of these companies, to appoint three directors of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and three directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN AND GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Will they be railway men?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN AND GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
They will he men of high .standing. I am not in a jfosition yet to give their names, but they will be men who can be depended upon to watch the interest of the Government in connection with the administration of these railways. The reason why we propose this is, as I have stated, that we are making these loans upon tenuous security. It is, therefore, in our view, important that we should be completely informed through our own representatives upon the two boards of directors' as to the condition and administration of these railways from time to time until the report has been made by the experts whom we shall engage to make an investigation into the whole Canadian railway 'Situation for the purpose which I have mentioned.
We propose also to provide for a continuous audit of the revenues and expenditures of these two railway systems. We have provided items in the Estimates for the purpo.se of defraying the expenses of the board of investigation which I have mentioned, and also of the continuous audit. As a result of the appointment of such auditors and our directors upon the boards of the two Tailway companies, we

expect to be kept thoroughly informed as to their administration and condition.
I have shown the present condition of the companies. I have pointed out that there are three alternatives, and three only namely, liquidation, taking over by the Government of the systems in question, or the affording of temporary assistance pending a solution of the larger question. The first alternative would, as I have stated, be at this juncture a most serious calamity and a great blow to the public credit and standing of the Dominion abroad. The second would add exceedingly heavy burdens to the increasing financial burden of the war, and would, I believe, seriously embarrass us in providing for its further financing on the increased scale to which we are looking forward. The third alternative, and the one which we propose, maintains the situation as it is at present and gives us time to investigate the whole problem with a view to such action at the next session of Parliament as may, it is to be hoped, solve in a permanent fashion Canada's railway difficulties. It seems to us that the latter course is unquestionably the course of wisdom, and I earnestly hope that the proposals of the Government looking to this end will meet the approval and endorsation of the House and of the country.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (South Renfrew):	Mr. 'Speaker, I do not propose
to deal with this proposition in any detail, because I have not had time to look at the figures, having only received them to-day. I would suggest to the Minister of Finance that we might go into committee, and then take up some other business in order to give us an opportunity at least until tomorrow of looking into the matter. As I received a copy of the Canadian Northern report only about twenty minutes ago, I have not had time to read it over.
The difficulty that confronts the members and the House is this: How long, O Lord, how long? It does not need any arguments or figures to convince the members of this House that they want to do what is right for the Dominion of Canada, they want to do that which will have no bad effects on our financial position. But that is the argument that has been used for years and years. When we are discussing these things we are met with the suggestion that if this aid is not given something terrible is going to happen to the country. It is really em-

barrassing to know just what is the best thing to do,-we have done it so often. On several occasions we have been assured that this is the last time of asking; and the aid has gone through; and the very next morning after the Governor General has signed the measure, movements have begun for requests for another grant or some additional aid. Another difficulty that strikes me just now after hearing the Minister of Finance is this-that we are not absolutely sure on what ground this aid is needed. In the first place we have not all the figures about the Canadian Northern revenue and expenditure, and cost of operation. And, secondly, it looks as if one of the great incentives to the granting of aid to the Grand Trunk Pacific is that the Grand Trunk does not want to do it. These things just struck me casually. Is it p'ossible that if this Parliament did not give aid the Grand Trunk would still decline to give it? I know that the shareholders' of the Grand Trunk have been objecting for two or three years to giving further aid to the Grand Trunk Pacific. But so have the people of Canada been objecting to giving further aid to anybody. Is it outside the range of possibility that if we did not give it the Grand Trunk would have to give it?
I want a little time to look into these matters before I come to a decision. It is true that speaking generally seventy-five per cent of the railways of America have been in liquidation at one time or another -perhaps the percentage is greater than that. But what we have to do is to make sure that the interests of the people for whom these railways are constructed shall be protected. I am not sure that the interests of the people of the United States have not been as fully protected by having the railways go into liquidation, as they would have been otherwise. Of course, they have not aided railways, as a government, so much as we have. The statement appears in a British Columbia newspaper, and I would like to ask the Minister of Finance about it, that legislation here will have the effect of relieving the British Columbia Government of its obligation to the Canadian Government. I cannot think there is any foundation for that, but it is stated in the report of a deliverance of a public man in British Columbia. Of course, if we are to assume the liabilities of the provinces and other creditors, let us take over the railways at once. It is true, as the minister has stated,

that the war conditions have made it difficult to raise money. It is also true that the low rate of interest at which some of these securities were issued has made it impossible, no doubt, to realize nearly as much upon them as would have been realized had not the rate of interest risen, due to war conditions.
Let me go back to my original question: How long is it to continue, if Parliament grants this aid? The Minister of Finance tells us that there are three things that face us. As he states them they amount to this-liquidation, nationalization, and procrastination. Now, there may be things that have greater terrors than liquidation of a railway company under present conditions. Possibly it would not be a terrible calamity if nationalization took place-for what is proposed is only an expedient, a temporary arrangement, even at the best; the situation has to be faced, and faced before very long. Should we temporize, should we keep on putting off and putting off?-particularly, when it is such an expensive pastime? The minister says, and says with a good deal of force, that it would be a bad time to assume all the liabilities that these two railway companies have upon them. But would it? Are we not assuming them now? Are we not in the position, as a Parliament, of assuming the liabilities of these two companies to a very large extent?-and having nothing to show for our liability at that. If we were to go further, although we should, perhaps, assume a heavier liability, still, we should have some property to show for our liability, we should have the railway property at least to the extent of the liability, if it were worth the money. As we go on now, we are handing out money year after year, and have nothing to show for it except forty-five per cent of the Canadian Northern stock-

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN AND GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Forty per cent.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN AND GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Forty per cent of the
Canadian Northern stock, which, I imagine, would not make anybody rich on the stock exchange at the present time.
Now, coming to the Grand Trunk Pacific. I think I told the Minister of Finance once in a quiet way that a certain report issued must have the effect of making it difficult for the Grand Trunk to obtain money; and, from the day the 'Staunton-Gutelius report was issued by this Government, the company began to have difficulty in securing money. I pointed out that that would be the only serious result of the report. For
whether such statements be true or not, capital is very sensitive and shies at the least provocation, and sometimes without any provocation.
Now, perhaps I should not say what I am about to say, but I think I am justified in saying it from the position I have taken with the Grand Trunk people. They will understand that I am not saying anything hew. That company will never make a success of its lines in Canada if it continues to operate them at long range. We in Canada are moving along so rapidly, as a new country, that the situation of yesterday is not the same as that of to-day and the situation of to-day may not be that of tomorrow. If any concern, a transportation company particularly, wishes to grapple with situations as they arise, it must have its directing forces on the ground. It is not so in the old land, where, conditions are the Tesult of centuries of work and development. We change in a day-in a few hours; what is a good policy now may not be a good policy to-morrow. The Canadian Pacific Railway has its board in Canada and can control its affairs. It can meet at 10 a.m., decide on a policy, and at 11 a.m. put it into force; in fact, it often puts the policy into force and meets afterwards. But as' to the Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific, while in a measure it manages its affairs in Canada, the fact is that no departure of any importance can take place, no real advancement can be made, without first submitting it to the board in London.
By the time that is received by that board and is studied as it necessarily must be, and reply is made to the Canadian management, the reason for the application has disappeared and the next order of business is at hand. Under these circumstances the application might as well never have been made, because the time has passed for it to be acted upon. While the Grand Trunk people in London are wondering what they are going to do, the Canadian Pacific railway, because it has the power, steps in and takes action. One of the difficulties in connection with the management of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway is that while it is the best main line of road on the American continent, it has not sufficient branch lines to feed it and give it the business that it ought to have. That neglect will be more marked as the years go by, unless it be remedied. I know that the management in Canada did endeavour time after time to make as rapid progress as could be made, but these things all had to be submitted

to the board in London, and by the time that board had made reply the Canadian Pacific railway had its men working on a branch line, and the Grand Trunk Pacific branch lines were not needed; they would be superfluous. I think it is the duty of the Government to tak-e the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk management to one side-I do not mean the Canadian end of the management, I mean Itlhe home end-have a quiet talk with them, and tell them that so long as the control is 4,000 miles away from the railway, so long will its management be inefficient and its financing almost impossible. I discussed this with Mr. Smithers on two or three occasions-and I am not saying anything now that I have not said to him most emphatically. The difficulty with the Grand Trunk Pacific system, as I pointed out to him, is not the matter of management; it is financial. The greatest financial mind obtainable should have been secured years ago by this company, and should have been on the ground in the Dominion of Canada, knowing the conditions, knowing what to recommend, and having power to act quickly on that recommendation. I submilt that, no matter what happens, if the Grand Trunk Pacific is to remain as a company-managed road, the body having control must be removed to Canada, or the road never can be successful.

speechtext: Well, if it had come all the way East and had connected its western .system with the seaboard on the east, or with tide water at Quebec, making arrangements with the Government railway to go to Halifax and St. John, it would have been somewhat behind; but I submit that its greatest difficulty has been in trying to finance the road through and west of the Rocky mountains. This was discussed between the Canadian Northern Railway proprietors and myself on several occasions, and the position I always took with them was this: Ultimately you will have a transcontinental line undoubtedly, because you will want a western outlet as well as an eastern outlet; but for the time being, unltil you get your system in the Prairie Provinces connected with the East, do not go farther west; by the time you have that done, if Canada is going to be what we think, the conditions will enable you to judge of the feasibility of going through to the West. Mark you, that was not with any 'antipathy of their going to the western coast; that was for the purpose of keeping the enterprise on a sound footing as it went along, and I believe that had that been done, to-day the Canadian Northern railway, with at most very small aid, would have been able to finance itself, and we would not have had this continual coming, year after year, and this constant repetition of votes to aid this enterprise. subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN AND GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
As my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) desires some further information, and also a further opportunity to examine the documents which have been laid on the table of the House, I have only a few words to say now. This is an important subject, and it is manifestly only fair to postpone the discussion as he requests. There are, however, one or

two things I should like to say before the House goes into committee. One is that thirteen years ago, on the 18th day of next August, I asked the late Government, our predecessors, to make that very stipulation which the hon. gentleman now says should have been made; that is to say, that there should be from Edmonton west to the coast only one line of railway, common to the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern Railway. That would have avoided what might perhaps be regarded as an economic waste, and would have effected a saving of from $75,000,000 to $100,000,000. I made some further suggestions, which I shall be prepared to debate with my hon. friends when the time comes, to indicate to them that the situation which has arisen to-day is one for which they are very largely, if not wholly responsible. Every hon. gentleman in this House knows precisely ' the conditions that confronted us when we came into power in October, 1911 -two great transcontinental railway systems, both having received the imprimatur of the Government as such by statutes of this country, both uncompleted, and both of them impossible of completion unless assistance should be given. It would be proper to leave the consideration of that until my hon. friend has made himself familiar with the details of the present proposals. He asks about the condition of the Canadian Northern Railway line; he inquires who the directors will be and what part they will take. I may tell him that they will be men who will command the confidence of the country, and further than that, I have no doubt that they will take such part in the management of these roads as will be consistent with their duty as representatives of the interests of this ' country in connection with further construction, and with the operation of the two railways.
I pass by my hon. friend's suggestion that the difficulties which confront the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to-day are due to the fact that an investigation was made by the present Administration, after it came into power, into the construction of the road. That remark could not have been made by my hon. friend in any very serious spirit. As a matter of fact, the Grand Trunk Railway has been carrying on the financing for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway since its construction was first undertaken in 1904 or 1905. The conditions that confront the Grand Trunk

Pacific Railway to-day have been described by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. The conditions which confront that road are in no way due to any report that was made or any investigation that was held. As a matter of fact, the Government have sought to co-operate in every possible way with the Grand Trunk in maintaining the stability and the financial credit of the Grand Trunk Pacific enterprise from the day we came into power. It is true that the enterprise was launched under conditions of which the opposition of the day did not approve. It is perfectly true that we then made certain suggestions which were not adopted, and the value of which I -shall be prepared to discuss before this debate is -concluded. It ie equally true that, as the proposals of the Government of that day were ratified by Parliament, as they were afterwards approved by the people of this country, we felt it our duty, when we came into power, to so guide our policies and our conduct as to support that enterprise in exactly the same .way as we would have supported it had we been responsible for it in the first instance. In doing that we were doing no more than was proper and necessary, having regard to the principles of constitutional government which control such conditions. As an example of the extent to which we have gone in endeavouring to support the -enterprise which was launched by my hon. friends opposite when they ware in power, I may say that for the period of nearly four years that the Grand Trunk Pacific has been in operation in the Prairie Provinces, and for the year that it has been in operation through the mountains, it has been maintained, so far as the payment of interest is concerned, upon a construction -basis which permitted interest to be paid out of capital. For that reason, the affairs of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway have not been in the limelight to the same extent as the affairs of the Candian Northern Railway.

Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Minister of Finance a question or two for information. What reason 'have we to believe that this statement of Canadian Northern railway affairs is an absolutely correct statement, covering all their liabilities? For my part, I do not believe that the Canadian Northern aTe in a position to state what their liabilities are. I do not believe that they know what their position is. I would suggest that when we take (the matter up again my hon. friend should give us -so-me information as to what amount of money, in addition to the present liabilities of the company will be required to put the company on a commercial basis; that is, to put it where it can carry freight cheaply and perform the duties for which it was organized. For instance, in my part of the country they have a branch line which was practically idle all last winter, and it will take a great deal of expenditure on many of their branch lines to put them in shape -so that they can meet operating expenses and pay interest on their indebtedness. In dealing with the question we should have some such information which would certainly be a very great help to us when we come to consider what ought to be done in connection with the proposals made by the Government. I would also like some information on this point: If we are going to finance this company, what will be the policy of the Gov-

eminent in regard to this company extending their field Still further by purchasing o.r building lines and extending in a manner that makes it impossible for them to concentrate their energies on the part of the country which they now occupy.

To enable us to understand this question, I think the Minister of Finance ought to give the House some information as to how this amount of $15,000,000 was arrived at, and as to the purposes for which At is to be used. The minister has ashed the House to accept the statement that he made an examination, and that he was satisfied that $15,000,000 was the smallest amount which could be given to enable the Canadian Northern Railway Company to go on. I think that information ought to be given now, so that the House and the country might understand. While I am on my feet, may I be permitted (to point out the singular method which the Government has adopted in presenting this matter for the consideration of Parliament. I think that this is the first occasion on which any Government has come to Parliament asking for such a large sum as $23,000,000 for two railway companies, and submitting it in the Estimates, without making the matter one of special legislation as it should be. There should have been a concrete Bill so that the proposals now submitted to Parliament could be reviewed and dealt with, and the legislation considered and enacted, if it is to be enacted, by the Government in accordance with precedent. There are reasons, I have no doubt, why the Government has gone outside the usual method of presenting legislation, and put these proposals in the Estimates. When my hon. friend the Minister of Finance dilated upon the condition of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and upon the position of this country at the present time, he simply stated what hon. gentlemen on this side of the House declared two years ago would be the result of the loan of $45,000,000. It was pointed out distinctly and clearly, not only by hon. gentlemen on this side, but by hon. gentlemen supporting the Prime Minister, that when the Government provided that loan of $45,000,000 it put this country in a position of being liable for every dollar of debt that had been incurred by the Canadian Northern Railway Company, both prior and subsequent to the granting of that security. It was urged by the Government then that that was not so, that the situation was such that, in [DOT] 
order to enable the Canadian Northern to break through its financial difficulties, that loan of $45,000,000, even supposing it did leave $65,000,000 of liabilities still to be liquidated, would result in a condition of affairs in which the Government of this country would be relieved from further advances, and the company would be able to go on. To-day it is quite apparent-my hon. friend has told the House-that if the Government undertake to exercise the power contained in the mortgage, the result would be that we would be liable for every cent of this indebtedness, both prior and subsequent, including the floating liabilities. My hon. friend did not take advantage of the safeguard which they allege was of the most vital character at that time when they assured the House and the country that they proposed to appoint certain directors upon the Canadian Northern board. They gave us that assurance then, just as they are asserting to the country to-day, that they propose to provide safeguards for the future by putting a certain number of gentlemen on these railway boards. The statement was made to the House by the Government during the present session, that no director had ever been appointed by the Government to the Canadian Northern board to watch the interests of the country or guard the position of the Government after that loan was made two years ago. Why, therefore, are we to accept the statement of the hon. gentleman as being any vital guarantee that they are going to put three members on this board or that the interests of the country are going to be better protected in the future than they have in the past?

friend's point, but I do not appreciate the suggestion he makes as being any answer to the claim that, immediately after the passage of that legislation the Government should have put its representative on the board in order that the interests of Canada might be protected. The situation in which the Canadian Northern stands to-day, as far as one can gather from hurriedly looking over the statement, is the situation that has existed every moment during the past two years. It does not sieem possible for this Government to initiate any policy in regard to any matter without providing for the appointment of a commission to go out and report, or it may be, never report at all, because some of these commissions aTe allowed to die a natural death. Nobody has ever heard of their reporting if they have ever done so. My hon. friends now propose to appoint the 85th or 86th commission which they have appointed since they came into power to make inquiry as to what should be done in regard to this railway problem. It is like locking the stable door after the horse is stolen, my hon. friends two years ago should have had these commissioners appointed. The Minister of Finance, knowing the position of the Canadian Northern and the burden which the country assumed when it provided for a .loan to them of $45,000,000, should have taken up the question as to whether or not this country would be bound to assume this railway and nationalize it. It was the bounden duty of the Government to have done that two years ago. They are simply two years too late in dealing with this question, even assuming that the proposition brought down to-day is tenable in. the slightest degree.- The result has been that for two years Messrs. Mackenzie .and Mann have had control of the operation, the finances, and the securities of the Canadian Northern, and they have been able to do what they pleased in regard to them without the slightest interference, or restrictions, or caretaking of the situation by this Government in any w.ay. After two years of non-interference, after after two years of absolute failure to secure the interests of this country, or to make inquiries as to whether or not, or as to how, this road should be nationalized or taken over, the Minister of Finance tojday admits absolutely that they have done nothing; that we are up against the situation, which exists to-day and which has existed for two years, and that they have permitted control to remain in the hands which brought about 226
conditions which rendered interference necessary, .according to hon. gentlemen opposite, in 1914. After two years my hon. friend comes to-day and says: I am going to ask the House to give these gentlemen $15,000,000 more because this is the least they can get along with. He expects the House and the country to accept that. In these times of thrift, of economy and of care being enjoined upon the private individual by advertisements and by publications issued by the Government, the Government themselves are playing the part of spendthrifts. They have permitted this situation to arise, as the result of which $15,000,000 is to be taken out of the public treasury, and we are asked to await the report of a commission, which may never report, and which we isay is simply intended to postpone further action in the hope thait something or another may arise in the future. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is a situation which demands more information than we have before us. If my hon. friend can give us any better information than he has I think we ought to have it. I would ask him to give a further explanation of this proposed expenditure of $15,000,000 and a definition of the statement which he has submitted.

speechtext:
There is one .matter in regard to which the Minister of Finance has not given any reasonable information to the House, and I think be might be very well expected to do it in answer to my hon. friend from Pietou (Mr. Macdonald). My hon. friend from Pietou has called attention to the most extraordinary fact that probably for the first itime in the history of this country an appropriation of this character was made by placing it in the Estimates instead of coming before Parliament with a resolution



followed by a Bill so that the details might be discussed, and so that any amendment might be made which the committee would deem desirable. We have here, in the ordinary Estimates submitted to Parliament, a proposal to make a loan of $8,000,000 to the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the only condition which is attached to it is that the disposition of the loan is to be subject to the direction of the Governor in Council. We have also a similar provision with respect to a proposed loan of $15,000,000 to the Canadian Northern. I say, Sir, it is unheard of in the history of this Parliament that a proposition of that kind should be submitted simply as an ordinary Estimate. That there must he some peculiar reason for it is apparent, because with respect to what is known as the Quebec and Saguenay railway, a proposal which is only going to involve some $4,000,000, the Government does not put it in the Estimates in the ordinary way, but the Acting Minister of Railways and Canals has introduced a Bill, which appears to-day on the Order Paper, to acquire that railway. The proper course, it seems to me, would have been for the Minister of Finance to submit a resolution in the ordinary form authorizing the Government to make this loan, and then to follow that up with a Bill, giving the regular authority of the Governor General in Council. The reason for the course adopted ought to be stated to the House.
Some condition, I think, ought to be attached to this loan. In 1914, when the question of giving $45,000,000 aid by guarantees to the Canadian Northern Railway Company was under consideration, I ventured to call attention to the fact that the time might come when it would be deemed in the interest of the country to take over the whole Canadian Northern Railway system and to operate it as a Government railway. I called attention to the fact that the company was admittedly in a bad condition financially, and that unless the country came to its aid at that time to the enormous amount of $45,000,000, it would be compelled to go into the hands of a receiver. I urged that, as the company was proposing that the Government should come to its assistance to that enormous extent, some provision should be made whereby the country could for a reasonable sum, take over this system in the future. I pointed out that the Government ought not to give the requisite assistance to tide this company over its financial difficulties until the day of pros-

perity would arrive, without some provision whereby, if the country decided to acquire the system in the future, it would not be mulcted in an enormous amount for the equities which Mackenzie and Mann would have in the system. If I remember rightly, I moved a resolution at that time fixing the amount at which the country would be entitled to take over the road, at a maximum of $30,000,000, and that resolution was put to a vote of the House. My hon. friend the Solicitor General made the statement at that time, that Messrs Mackenzie and Mann, ratheT than accept the sum of $30,000,000 for their equity in this road, would allow the whole system to go into liquidation.	Upon what	authority	my hon.	friend made that
statement I do not know, but it struck me as an extraordinary statement that those gentlemen, in a condition, as they alleged, practically of bankruptcy at that time should refuse to fix as a maximum a sum of $30,000,000, which at 5 per cent would give to each of those men and his heirs the magnificent sum of $750,000 per year, or upwards of $2,000 per day, and that they would prefer to throw the whole system into liquidation to accepting it. This company comes again and says to this Government:	Again we are practically bankrupt; again we say to you we cannot continue the operation of this road unless you come to our assistance. Is the Government going to go to their relief again without fixing any maximum sum in case the country should wish to take the road over in the future? The Minister of Finance says that the question of nationalization will come up very soon. The Minister of Public Works, giving us the benefit of a very eloquent address the other evening upon the whole railway system of Canada, stated that the whole question of nationalization would soon come up. Are we going to advance this at present bankrupt concern $15,000,000 in addition to the $45,000,000 guaranteed in 1914 and to the other assistance which has been given, so as to tide it over until a day when prosperity again may come to it, and then be obliged, in order to acquire the system and to nationalize the railway, to give Mackenzie and Mann, not $30,000,000, but practically whatsoever they choose to ask? Does not the Minister of Finance think this is the time to fix the terms upon which this country may take over the Canadian Northern railway should we decide to do so? I submit this for the consideration of my hon. friend. While it

is "true he does not give us a very great opportunity to present amendments, yet I think that is an amendment which he himself ought to propose, so that if the country should decide to take over this system, it may know that the system will be taken over on reasonable terms.
I was surprised at the bravery of my right hon. friend the- Prime Minister, coming to this House with a proposition which I would think he would like to see treated in a non-partisan spirit, asking for this extra lgeislation, that he should seek to provoke party feeling in the speech which he has made. Instead of accepting, as I would have thought my right hon. friend would accept the responsibility for that part of the Canadian Northern railway system which is involving this country in the most tremendous part of its liability, namely, the construction of the road through the mountains of British Columbia, my right hon- friend seeks to throw upon the Liberal party the whole responsibility for the disastrous condition in which the country finds itself to-day in respect to the Canadian Northern. Upon what ground does he - do so? Why, he says, I think it is thirteen years ago since I proposed to the then Government that they should provide that there should be only one line of railway through British Columbia to be used jointly by the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern. Let us see whether my right hon. friend is right in saying that the refusal of the then Government to provide for that is the cause of the present situation. Does he forget that in the Transcontinental Railway Act, it is expressly provided that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company shall allow to any other company the use of its rails subject to an agreement to be made by approval of the Governor General in Council, and that under that the Canadian Northern Railway Company might and would necessarily have been allowed the use of the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific from Edmonton through to the Pacific coast. The very thing which my right hon. friend says he thought should be provided is provided for in the agreement for the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific. The late Government refused to grant a subsidy to the Canadian Northern to buikl its railway west of Edmonton. The Government thought-and I think wisely-that they should not go ahead with the new transcontinental line through the Rocky mountains, but should allow the system to 226* .
be developed, allowing the road to get into a position of financial strength before attempting this hazardous enterprise of building through the mountains to the coast. But when this Government came into power, it worked in harmony with Sir Richard McBride, then Premier of British Columbia, who seemed to think that there would be no limit to the wealth and the money which British Columbia could throw into this great enterprise, and he gave a very large subsidy for the road through the Rocky mountains, joining with the Government of British Columbia when that Government guaranteed bonds upon this road to the extent of nearly $40,000,000. Those members of this House who have been in British Columbia and who have gone over the line of the Canadian Pacific or of the Canadian Northern railway, know . that for nearly two hundred miles those two railways run parallel to each other, one upon one side of the Fraser river and the other upon the other side, and that for at least one hundred and fifty miles through that portion of the mountains of British Columbia, there is no reasonable possibility of any traffic whatever to feed the Canadian Northern railway. And yet the hon. gentleman seeks to throw the responsibility for this useless and most expensive construction upon the Liberal party, which refused to countenance any proposition to extend the Canadian Northern through the mountains, but took authority for the use of the Grand Ttunk Pacific line through the mountains should it be desired to afford that connection.

I notice that the facts are as I stated them to be, that there are to-day four regiments besides the Universities Regiment, that is five altogether, being recruited at Edmonton at the moment, besides two others at full strength; and I am satisfied that there are others being recruited there. I know there was recruiting for a regiment to be known as the Bantams of Vancouver, at Edmonton. They may have ceased their operations at Edmonton now. This fact demonstrates that no discrimination whatever is used in the securing of recruits, in the way of having regard to the requirements of civil life; that the department simply goes after recruits whenever and wherever it can get them, without regard to any other circumstance. And more than that, the fact that so many units are being recruited in the same place at the same time tends against the success of the work. There is instituted a spirit of competition between the different officers who are engaged in recruiting that does not tend to success. I admit that probably to have two battalions recruiting at the same time and in the same place may give a healthy measure of competition; but when more than two are recruited it certainly is injurious rather than beneficial. I think it is only fair to draw the attention of the minister to my opinion in regard to that. I have done so in view of the number of men recruited in Edmonton and the number of branches of the service for which they have been recruited. I may claim to speak for a part of the country that has shown as good a military spirit as any other.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think that is eminently true. My hon. friend no doubt has in mind that these regiments are recruited, I suppose, from a considerable district around Edmonton. I remember one which went through not long ago whose members had come to a considerable extent from the Peace river country. There has been an endeavour in some cases at least,
to my certain knowledge, to adjust the recruiting to the requirements of local conditions. I cannot recall that any representations ever came to my attention concerning Edmonton, but I do recall other cases; and in those cases- an endeavour was made by the department to meet local conditions through the guidance of recruiting officers.

If I may be permitted, I would like to refer to something that came up when this item was under discussion on Saturday. I discussed what had happened to the 9th Battalion recruited at Edmonton, and I informed the committee of the fact that the colonel who had recruited that battalion, and who had been colonel of the original volunteer battalion out of which the 9th Battalion was formed, had been displaced by Colonel Maynard Rogers, formerly of Ottawa, and that under Colonel Maynard Rogers' command the battalion had been broken up and had not been sent to the front as a unit. The men themselves, their relatives and friends, and the community from which they came, certainly felt a great sense of grievance, and they believe that Col. Maynard Rogers was in large measure responsible for that result. To-day I have been favoured with a letter from General Hughes, enclosing a letter from Colonel Rogers to myself, in which both General Hughes and Colonel Rogers take exception to the statements I made. I will not trouble the House by reading the letters; I will just draw attention to one paragraph in General Hughes' letter. He says:
Permit me to say you are entirely in error, and that Colonel Osborne was relieved on account of his incapacity, and by my direction.
I am not going to discuss Colonel Osborne; I do not know whether he was capable ot incapable; but I do know that he was the means of raising a regiment, one of the first regiments to reach Val-cartier, and that, to that degree, he certainly rendered good service to his country, and, in all fairness, I think, was entitled to some consideration. I do not suggest that, because Colonel Osborne was successful in raising a regiment, he would therefore be a competent military commander in the field. I do not say that any injustice was done to Colonel Osborne by his being retired, but I do say that when the Department of Militia, or the Government, saw fit to replace Colonel Osborne by Colonel Rogers, and that then under the command of Colonel Rogers that battalion was not considered fit to take the field, I am compelled to reach the conclusion that Colonel Rogers was not competent. At any rate, without discussing the matter at any greater length, General Hughes and Colonel Rogers will have to divide between them the responsibility for the fact which resulted in: such a tremendous disappoint-

ment to the men who had enlisted in that battalion, .to their relatives and friends, and to the community from which they came, by reason of its being broken up, disbanded practically, or attached to other units, thus being deprived of the privilege of going forward as an Edmonton battalion which was of course their desire. The men did go forward as members of other units, and casualty lists show that they played their part as other men played their parts. We arc not complaining, because they volunteered to render service in the Empire's cause; they were privileged to render that service, hut there is a certain reasonable measure of consideration to which men and officers are entitled, and which they certainly did not receive in this case. In his letter General Hughes says that I am attacking Colonel Rogers. I have no desire to attack Colonel Rogers; it is a condition of facts of which I complain. Colonel Rogers in his letter also seems to suggest that I am attacking him. I repeat that I have no desire to attack Colonel Rogers. But I do desire to place before the House the fact that every man in the 9th Battalion, and his right to take his part in the cause for which he volunteered, is just as important to me as Colonel Rogers or General Hughes. I do not propose to allow such an occurrence to pass without due notice in this House, even though Colonel Rogers, and even General Hughes, may consider it in some degree a reflection on them. I have no desire to reflect on either of them, but I make a statement of fact, and that fact was certainly most unpleasant and most injurious to the men who were concerned, and to the locality from which they came.
It is a fact that that occurrence has not prevented further recruiting in Edmonton; it is a fact that the patriotism of the people, not of Edmonton alone, but of the country surrounding,' is such that they are prepared to come forward and offer themselves even although they do not get that recognition which they have a right to expect. But I must point out to the minister that while that may he the case in Edmonton, it is not likely to be the case throughout the country. When an instance,, such as I speak of, occurs in Edmonton- and I think it must be admitted that it was a most aggrevated instance-similar instances may have occurred in other places; and when we comment, as sometimes people do comment, upon the slackness of recruiting in different localities, perhaps such incidents may have some-

thing to do with it. I say it would be well for those who are responsible for the conduct of our affairs to see that such incidents do not occur, and to see that no reason is given to cause such a sense of disappointment and unfairness amongst the men as would tend to prevent others from offering themselves for service. When a man offers himself, with the sacrifice of his time, his position, and even his life, he is surely entitled to a square deal. If he does not get it he and his friends feel a sense of injustice.
There is another instance I desire to draw attention to. The 3rd C.M.R. was not from Edmonton city, but from the country east of Edmonton. Major Fane, the commander of the unit, came from Veg-reville. The unit went into action some time in December of last year. They suffered very heavy casualties; I think one-third of them were killed and wounded in one day's operations. One of the officers was killed and the major was very badly wounded. They were very severely cut up. As far as I am aware, they conducted themselves with all credit; and our authorities showed their regard for the services rendered by this unit by wiping them out. There is no 3rd C.M.R. now. The unit has ceased to exist because it has been distributed among other forces just as the 9th battalion was. I do not think that such a system as that is good for the service, I do not think it is to the advantage of recruiting, nor do I think it is creditable to anybody who is concerned in it. Right from the start as far as, our experience goes, no regard whatever has been paid to locality in the matter of recruiting, no regard has been paid to the establishment of fixed units attached to a certain locality where the presence of friends might tend to hold men together and give them a- certain spirit in carrying on their operations. No regard has been paid to that and, due to that fact, we perhaps in a very large measure feel a certain slackness in recruiting that is complained of in a great many cases. In our own case we had three battalions training at Edmonton for the greater part of a year, one of them for over a year. From all of these battalions drafts were sent-two drafts from the 51st and one each from the 63rd and 66th. I do not know where they went or what units they were attached to. No doubt they are serving their country, no doubt they are fighting in the same cause as if they were called the Edmonton or the Alberta battalions, but this is not a good way to inspire our population with a desire
for service. Every consideration should be given to the question of sentiment and it is well to encourage the idea of community of interest among the people of a certain locality. If a certain battalion is known as an Edmonton battalion, or an Alberta battalion, if it is recruited from Edmonton or Alberta, when the men who belong to it go forward, every one concerned, those who remain behind and those who have gone forward, have an interest in what that battalion is doing that he otherwise would nolt have had, and the ignoring of that fact has tended very greatly against rapid recruiting in many parts of the country. It is true that we have done magnificently in the way of recruiting. We have, as the right hon. the Prime Minister has said, raised over 300,000, but we have to raise 200,000 more. It must be remembered that raising the last 200,000 is a very different matter from raising the first 200,000, because the same conditions that produced the first 200,000 do not exist in connection with the last 200,000. Now that we are coming to the point when there is an abundance of employment, when every man who joins must certainly leave a lucrative position, we are facing a situation in connection with which we must recognize all those motives and sentiments that tend towards a willingness to sacrifice for the good of the cause. This 'has not been done in the past. We have done well without it, but we cannot expect to ooi!-tinue to do well and to carry on the bisi-ness in that way. When we claim to have raised 300,000, that means that we have included in that number the rejections, which have been stated as over 20,000. That is not a fair count. 'These men mav have been enlisted, but they have been rejected, they are not part of our forces, and we have no right to count them as [DOT]simply enlisted. We must counit only the men who either have rendered service, or are actually on the road to service.

I wish to bring before my hon. friend the Prime Minister, while he is acting as Minister of Militia and Defence, a subject that has been communicated to me by a gentleman living in my own constituency, a gentleman of some standing and repute, who has been warden of the county, and, for many years, reeve of the township in which he resides, Mr. James Donaldson. Mr. Donaldson writes me that the Militia Department has promulgated an order that soldiers may assist

the farmers for a certain time during the present spring. In tfhe city of Stratford, in the county that I have the honour to represent, there is located the 110th Battalion, probably recruited up to 700 or 800. This order apparently is applied to that battalion and the men have gone into the country districts to work. This gentleman points out (that the season has been very wet and backward, and that while the soldiers have been, and are now, engaged amongst the farmers, the spring work has hardly commenced owing to the wet nature of the ground, and he has asked me to bring the matter up and suggest that the time be extended. I may observe here that what is true in my district may be true elsewhere in Canada and I would therefore request the militia authorities to consider, having regard to the condition of the land throughout every portion of the country, whether the time should not be extended and that, if any action is to be taken, an early announcement of it, almost forthwith if possible, should be made in order that disturbance would not be the outcome of it.

I would like to take advantage of this opportunity to say that the Government is authorizing the recruiting of a number of French Canadian battalions. A French Canadian battalion is being recruited as far west as Edmonton. It would be a great mistake to imagine that French Canadians are recruited only in the province of Quebec. A large number of my constituents hav-e been drafted into New Brunswick battalions, and a large number of French Canadians have been drafted into Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island battalions. The same is true of Ontario; in fact, in some of the battalions recruited in Ottawa some of the companies consist of French Canadians, and the same is true throughout Canada. Recruiting in the province of Quebec has perhaps not been as large as it should be, due to various causes, but I think it would be unfair to cast aspersions upon those who have enlisted and who are doing their duty splendidly at the front, because recruiting has perhaps not been as large as it should have been. I think that if proper measures are taken, recruiting can be increased in the province of Quebec; I think the Government has undertaken the recruiting of men in certain mral parts of the province.

I think it was

I think the committee
will agree with me that that is a very large sum for the amount of work that is being done. I want to point out to my right hon. friend, who is now Acting Minister of Militia, how to a certain extent the account has been run up to such a high figure. My information is-and I am satisfied that it is fairly correct-that in one company of Hussars, the horses are not owned by the Government, but are hired, and that the Government pays 50 cents a day for each horse, and, of course, the expenses and the keep of the horses; that a good many of the horses are horses that cost about $120 in that locality, and that the owner of each horse has the payment' in full of his horse in eight months; or, if a horse costs $150'he would receive the total value of it in ten months, so that those who have had horses hired to the Government from the outbreeak of the war have collected already about double their value. My information is that some of the officers own a number of horses and are therefore making a very considerable revenue and running up the cost of the guarding of the canal over and above what it would be if the Government followed its usual course and owned the horses that those men are using-
There is another matter that I think accounts to a slight extent for the very high cost of protecting that canal, and that is that with 120 men stationed at Morrisburg, there are 16 officers, or one officer for fewer than eight men. If that is the case-and I
am assured it is-it is a most unsatisfactory state of affairs, and I am drawing it to the attention of the acting minister in order that he may look into it and see if that is so, because I can hardly believe it.

Before the Chairman of the War Purchasing Commission answers by hon. friend with regard to that matter I would like to say that I understand there are not many horses employed on the canal. There are a few mounted men required. The arrangement, I believe, is that the owner provides the stabling and tabes care of ithe horse; the department provides the fodder, and I think the rate is what my hon. friend has suggested. I will have the matter looked into .and see whether the expense can be reduced.
With regard to the patrolling, I am informed by the deputy minister that every patrol on the canal must be in charge of an officer, and .some times .a patrol consists of only eight or ten men. The work has to be carried on day and night. I do not know about the particular district to which my hon. friend has alluded, bult I do know something about the work which was carried on in the vicinity of the Niagara peninsula, because I inspected some of the posts there last summer. The work is important and has to be attended to with a great deal of diligence, and if my hon. friend were made acquainted with all the intimations that have come to us from time to time a.s to the danger at this, that, or the other point, he would feel with us, I am sure, that even if the expense be pretty large, the Government ought not to relax any reasonable precautions. A lack of vigilance at some particular place, even for a very short time, might result in great destruction of property. lit has been held that the.se precautions ought to be of the most efficient character possible.

I have no intention of
suggesting that precaution should be relaxed in any way. My information is that men going out on patrol go two men at a time for two hours and patrol three miles and back. Possibly it may be that a larger proportion of officers are necessary. However, I am quite satisfied to have drawn the matter to the attention of the minister,

and I feel sure that if unnecessary expense is being incurred an effort will be made to curtail it.
