competition, it was divided into units, so that the clothing manufacturers could become interested, and the saving has been very great.

There is a vote of
$800,000 for clothing this year. Is that clothing purchased through the War Purchasing Commission?

I understand that that vote is for clothing for the militia force. Last year there was no vote of that character ki clothing. I am inclined to think though I am not speaking by the book, and am not certain of the policy of the department, that the department will draw on the stores for that clothing. If not, they will need to buy it by tender, or have it made under the present contract with the department.
If this clothing is used by our army, why is it charged to the Militia Department, instead 01 xo the war vote like other munitions of war?

As I explained, this item of $800,000 to which the hon. member for Pic-tou has referred, is for the militia force. Therefore, it is in the militia Estimates. But the war appropriation vote is $250,000,000 which went through last week.

Is it the policy of
the department to go on with the training and issuing of clothing to the militia when nearly all have gone overseas? There is only a skeleton organization.
_ Sir ROBERT BORDEN:	That was explained when the item passed. No clothing has been bought for some time, and it is necessary to provide it now. Some of the militia are on active service. This may also provide some clothing for a force raised for home defence, as suggested, I think, by the hon. member for Edmonton, when we were discussing this matter a day or two ago.

At $20 a suit this
would provide for 40,000 men. There is not that number of our militia who have not gone overseas.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The information I have is that the money is needed to provide the militia, permanent and nonpermanent, with clothing and necessaries. No vote for this purpose was taken in 191516 and consequently provision for 1916-17 is all the more necessary. The estimate of the Quartermaster General shows a total of over $1,000,000 but $800,000 will provide for present wants. I have details here of the number of caps and other articles in store. It does not follow that all this money will be used this year.

Will this clothing
be made by the contractors for the Militia Department?

The contractors for the
militia clothing am Mark Workman of Montreal and the Sanford Company. Their contract for militia clothing expires in 1917. They have been manufacturers, I believe, for a good many years past.
.Mr. DOUGLAS: I desire to draw the attention of the Prime Minister to a condition regarding recruiting which prevails in Edmonton. As he is aware the city of Edmonton and surrounding country has done a large amount of recruiting, and at present we have six battalions, a portion of which have not their full complement of men. I find a news item in an Edmonton paper which states that the 210th Battalion

of Mooeej-aw has opened a recruiting office in Edmonton. The item is as follows:
Captain J. L. Thomas, the recruiting officer for the 210th Battalion, with headquarters in Moose jaw, Sask., announces that an office for recruiting has been opened in Boom 5 in the Empire Block, corner of Jasper avenue and) 101st street. He also desires to contradict a report that has been set in circulation to the effect that this battalion is not an overseas unit. The 210th .has been authorized by Ottawa for mobilizaion in Moose jaw, Sask., and to recruit for overseas service in not only Saskatchewan, but Alberta also. Free transportation is given eligible recruits and owing to the fact that the men of this unit are either nearly all soldiers with previous active service o,r at any rate military training a much earlier departure for overseas is looked for than is usual. The 210th will put in their summer training at Sewell camp.
The point is that the province of Alberta has recruited more than her quota according to population in the overseas battalions. We have regiments not yet recruited to full strength. I understand that the policy of the department is not to authorize any new battalion until the battalions already authorized are up to strength. In view of that policy I think it is an injustice to Alberta, and to the city of Edmonton in particular, that an outside battalion with headquarters in Moosejaw should be permitted to have .its officers' come up and Tecruit soldiers from Alberta, pay transportation to Moosejaw, and take eligible men away who may be required to fill battalions at present being organized in Edmonton.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think there is a good deal of force in the hon. gentleman's suggestion. I will bring the matter to- the attention of the Adjutant General, who has control of such matters, and ask him to deal with it.
Would the Prime Minister he good enough to get from the department, for the information of the committee, a list of the various units, detachments and sections that have been recruited at Edmonton?	.

When I was home at Easter my attention was drawn to the fact that the railway bridges crossing the two branches of the Miramichi river were inefficiently protected, and I'was asked to draw the attention of the department to the fact-. In the event of any disaster happening through the action of an enemy, certainly transportation would be very much interfered with. I simply draw the attention of the department to the fact that
the interests of the country are more or less at stake through these bridges not being properly and efficiently patrolled.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I may say that my attention has been called to the matter. I communicated with the Department of Railways and Canals, and I understand that an intimation has come from the general manager that the subject is being dealt with.

Very good; we had better let the item stand.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at ei^ht o'clock, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.
Supplementary Estimates 1916-17. Railways and Canals-St. John terminal facilities-rebuilding grain elevator, $500,000.

Before taking up this item,
may I give some information which was asked for by the hon. member for Antig-onish (Mr. Chisholm) about the garden plot at Antigonish station. I wired to Moncton for the information and received this telegram in reply:
The loam used In making Antigonish garden plot was taken from our right of way near Malagash station. After four cars had been unloaded It was found that two carloads were suificient. As a result two cars were loaded back on the cars and shipped to Mulgrave, where it was used for similar purposes. The cost of loading done by regular sectionmen was about five dollars per car. The cost of reloading the two cars at Antigonish was approximately ten dollars.
F. P. Gautelius.

The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) asked me the date when the single fare for soldiers went into effect. I wired Moncton and have received this telegram from Mr. Hayes:
Your message fifth. Arrangements for single fare for soldiers on leave is generally in effect on Government railways. Frst arranged for Easter holidays. April twentieth to twenty-fourth inclusive and became generally effective April twenty-eight, it taking few days to print and distribute instructions to agents. If Mr. Macdonald has any instance where agents failing to carry out instructions would be pleased to investigate.
C. A. Hayes.
With reference to the item before us, the St. John elevator, the Intercolonial had an elevator at St. John which was destroyed by fire on August 13, 1914. It is the intention to build a transfer elevator at St. John, at Reid's point, with a capacity of about
500,000	bushels, which will serve a new slip. Conveyors would be extended to McLeod's and Pettinger's wharves. The object of locating at this point, instead of on the site of the old elevator, is to preserve the old site for yard accommodation. There is also .an item for $55,000 for the steamer Northumberland. This steamer has been plying between Prince Edward Island and Northumberland for a number of years. The company have disposed of their two vessels. The Northumberland was purchased by the Government for $55,000, and will now be operated .as part of the railway system.
What will be the capacity of the elevator to be erected?

The machinery of the elevator will have a capacity of 1,000,000 bushels, but the storage at first will be only 500,000 bushels. It is more of >a transfer elevator. We hope to get the 500,000 bushel elevator up before next winter, and it will then be easy to add as much additional capacity as we wish.
It seems to be a large price for an elevator of .small capacity.

The .initial cost of erecting an elevator is estimated at about $1 a bushel. That is largely for the machinery. Then, of course, when additional storage capacity is erected that costs much less in proportion, as the machinery is already installed. This will be done by tender, of course, and if we could have an elevator of 750,000 bushel capacity erected for $500,000 we should he very glad.

I quite agree that it is necessary to have this elevator, and I approve of the vote. My only criticism would he .as to the limited capacity of the elevator. What is the capacity of the Canadian Pacific railway elevator at St. John?

They have built a new elevator, with a capacity of one and a half millions, then there was an old elevator with a capacity of about one million. The difficulty with the Intercolonial has been that if we did (take grain to St. John we had no elevator of our own, and the Canadian Pacific railway always claimed that they had all the grain they could handle from their own line, and then, of course, there were the shunting charges across St. John, so that we were really not in a position to handle grain. Even with 500,000 bushels we would be able to handle quite a little outward-bound grain. In addition to that, if we come in on the St. John Valley road, we go right into the Canadian Pacific railway yards, and we will not have the heavy shunting charges.
Is the new elevator to be on the same side of the harbour as the Canadian Pacific railway elevators, or is it at Courtenay bay?

It is to be on the Courtenay bay or east side of the harbour. The Government own a lot of property, part of which they sold for a sugar refinery, and this is to be near the sugar refinery with carriers that will serve on the west side. It is on the east side of the harbour, but west of the elevator, and it will also serve Courtenay bay. It is intended to provide a storage capacity of more than 500,000 bushels, but we thought that if we could have
500,000	bushels capacity, and these vessels came next winter as they came last winter, we could put through a large quantity of grain by that transfer as well as by the transfer at Halifax.
Is it the intention of the Government to make the connections over the St. John Valley line with this elevator; is it part of the scheme?

Yes, we will go right over
that line.
This elevator is to be part of the new system of handling trade to St. John over the St. John Valley line?

Yes. As the hon. member
for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) stated the other

night, this route is 100 miles shorter than by the Canadian Pacific Railway. Of course, when we go over the eleven miles of the Canadian Pacific Railway we go through the Canadian Pacific Railway yards and right over to the Intercolonial terminals which are around Courtenay bay. We run right through to our own station. Our station will be on the east side, near where the other elevator was established.
Is this elevator accessible to the Intercolonial?
It is right on the .Intercolonial.

My only criticism would
be, first, that there might be a danger of the elevator not being built soon enough, and next that there is a very great probability of it not being big enough. To carry on the discussion, which we had with the minister some time ago, I would like to go on record as holding the view that it is absolutely necessary for the proper handling of the grain in the West over the Transcontinental line by all the year-round transit that there should be ample accommodation at the city of St. John, not merely sufficient to make a transfer of one or two cargoes, but to carry a considerable amount of grain as it is carried, though not to such a large extent, at the head of the lakes in storage. In order to -be of value in handling the grain, the railroad must bring it iorward as its rolling stock will permit, so many thousand bushels a day, or so many thousands a week. That quantity cannot be speeded up very much. The railways must carry the grain forward as their rolling stock will permit it to be carried forward, and, if there is not ample storage accommodation at the winter port, in the event of the iparket being depressed, or of vessels not being available, that movement by rail would have to cease until the small capacity transfer elevator at St. John was relieved; whereas if there was ample capacity at the St. John elevator that movement could be kept up continuously. That is the principle which I see in the successful handling of the grain of the Northwest, the possibility of keeping up a continuous movement by rail all the year round, m winter, as well as in summer. I am emphasizing this point because the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other night, and the Acting Minister of Railways to-night,
seemed rather to hold the view that there is no necessity for any considerable storage at the Atlantic 'winter port which is open and available to vessels all the year round, and that it might be supposed that the vessels would remove the grain as fast as it was brought in. In theory they would, but not in practice. The grain must go forward in a continuous stream, as the rolling stock of the railway will permit, and its transfer across the ocean then depends, partly on the condition of the market, and partly on the available ocean transport. There must be a large amount of storage accommodation, or that movement cannot take place in that way. My suggestion is that the minister get the biggest elevator he can for the money, and if he cares to double the amount, assuming that it is intended to transact business over the Transcontinental with the view of giving a continuous outlet of grain all the year round, he can go as far as he likes in elevatorbuilding at St. John, and I will be glad to support him.

The hon. member misunderstood me if he thinks that I was discussing this along the line that we did not require large storage capacity at the winter port. Years ago, in discussing this elevator question, I took the stand, and I think it was almost the unanimous opinion of the House, that we should have a large terminal storage capacity at our ocean ports. At that time it was Montreal that we had chiefly in mind, and at that time, I think, we had a capacity of only 1,000,000 bushels there. Now we have a capacity of 15,000,000 bushels, and a capacity of one and a half million bushels at Quebec. Last year, or probably two years ago, the capacity at St. John was increased by the establishment of a new elevator. We have now a capacity of one and a half million bushels in the new elevator, and, I think, a capacity of 1,000,000 bushels in the old elevator. I think we should have a great deal more accommodation, and no doubt it will have to be increased each year until we get a large capacity at St. John and Halifax. But I thought that we should have at once an elevator with a large capacity at Transcona, or at some other place in that section, and also that we should have one at once at St. John. In discussing the matter with the Minister of Finance, he asked me what I thought we would be able to get along with this year, that is, up till next spring, and I thought that if we could succeed in getting at each place a capacity of 500,000

bushels, then next year we could go on and extend it. I thought that that would be much better than building an elevator with a capacity of 1,000,000 bushels or
1.500.000	bushels at St. John without the small one at Winnipeg. The difficulty, I am informed by the management of the railway, is that they have to haul the grain to Fort William, which means a back haul on account of not having a transfer elevator at Winnipeg, where they could weigh the grain, inspect it, and give the certificates the same as is done at Saskatoon and Fort William. By having this elevator at a point where the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific meet, so that the grain could pass through the elevator and be weighed, and certified, the Transcontinental will save that back haul down to Fort William, and, on that account, be able to handle very much more grain. It will go right straight through to Armstrong, Quebec, St. John and Halifax. We will be in this position as far as the Intercolonial is concerned': If we can get this
500.000	bushel elevator up, we will have
1.250.000	bushels capacity between Halifax and St. John. That will put us in not a bad position to start with next fall. I do not think we can spend more than $1,000,000 between the two this year. At the same time I have tried to carry out the wishes of the Finance Minister (Sir Thomas White) that T should just place in the Estimates what I thought I could spend. If it overruns the amount a little, we may have to have a Supplementary Estimate next year but we will try and get as large a capacity as we can for this amount.
Did I understand the minister as telling my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) that the Intercolonial tracks now run to the point selected for the building of this elevator!

The hon. gentleman knows where the sugar refinery has been built. The track runs around and out to this point they call Reid's Point. The elevator is to be built in that vicinity near the sugar refinery. Then carriers can be run along the shore on the west side to it, and when Courtenay bay is developed so that vessels can get in there, carriers can go the other way. This elevator has only 500,000 bushels capacity. Of course, it will be extended on down towards the Courtenay bay side as well. . The management tell me that they think that would be bettor for the Intercolonial railway.
What I want to find out from the minister is whether the spur line Tunning from the Intercolonial track is already built to the point where the elevator will be?
At the present time a little line runs over there but when the Courtenay bay scheme is carried out, it will not be used as it now is. That is a new scheme altogether.

That is the Courtenay bay
scheme?
Yes, with the Courtenay bay scheme, there is a new way of coming in. The line we have now would never do for that.
Is there a way by which they can come in to that elevator until the Courtenay bay scheme is developed?
As soon as we can get sufficient work done on the Courtenay bay route, so that we can change the route to come in by Courtenay bay, we will do so. We have an amount in the Estimates for that work.

I understand that what the minister is proposing is that grain for export coming over the Transcontinental railway, will come down over the Transcontinental to McGivniey junction, then over the St. John Valley railway and the Canadian Pacific to St. John?
Yes.
And on through to this proposed elevator?
Yes.

Provided you want to take the grain over the Transcontinental railway to Moncton and, down over the Intercolonial to St. John, what connection have you to enable you to get these car loads of grain to the boats?
Just the same.

The link of the Valley railway from Gagetown to Westfield) is not supposed to be completed until the first of February, 1917, and it is very doubtful if all the contracts will be completed by that date; therefore, during this coming fall, the export grain which cannot go down by way of the Valley railway ought to go by Moncton and St. John.

Wje have that connection now and they are using it every day. We have a shunting engine that is kept busy shunt-

ing around there .now. That is where they load the lumlber and that is where the sugar refinery takes in its supplies.

Why should this elevator be charged to the Intercolonial railway when it is for the busines-s of the St. John Valley and Transcontinental ? Is it proposed to bring grain over the Intercolonial railway and not over the Transcontinental ? Why not build it as a Government elevator and1 allow either the Intercolonial or the other road to use it? There will be that capital ohaTge, or burden, upon the Intercolonial railway when it is for the use of another road unless you propose to allow the Intercolonial to make a profit out of the charges for handling the grain.

The Intercolonial always had an elevator. I never thought of that point. I thought it was simply replacing the old elevator that the Intercolonial had. I do not think it is a very serious matter. The hon. gentleman will see that in the next item we have an elevator charged against the Transcontinental railway.
But that is on the Transcontinental railway, and for the use of the T ranscontinental.
This is really on the Intercolonial Railway system.
But not for Intercolonial traffic.

It is partly for Intercolonial traffic. We propose to put this elevator on property which is owned and controlled by the Intercolonial railway. The St. John Valley road will go into the Intercolonial station and will use our terminals and yet it could not be called a part of the Intercolonial railway. I do not think that is a very serious point.

It is not very serious. I was to-day asked the question:	What
capital has been expended on the Intercolonial railway? The argument against the Intercolonial is based quite often on the amount of money that has been expended on capital account. Here is half a million being charged up to the Intercolonial railway although primarily it is not for Intercolonial traffic. This is only a unit, as I understand. Other units are to be added and in time we may have a further capital charge of a million and a half before we get through although it is to accommodate the traffic of another road.

There is a difference of
opinion in regard to that. It is to be on Intercolonial property and the Intercolonial should have an elevator anyway. It will have the use of the elevator.
Will there be any revenue for the Intercolonial railway from the traffic that is created through this elevator?

I do not suppose there will
be. If it goes through the yard of the Intercolonial railway there might be some but I do not know what the nature of the traffic would be there,

The Intercolonial gets
all the expense and none of the benefit.
I do not know what we could charge it too. We could only charge it to the Intercolonial or the Transcontinental railway.

You build elevators elsewhere and you do not charge them to the roads that the elevators are placed on. At St. John there will be just a plain elevator built and you can call it a Government elevator.

It adds to the value of the
property.

Certainly it does in a
way. I just raised the point because it seemed to me that it might perhaps have been overlooked. The Transcontinental railway will have the benefit of the elevator but it will be an expense to the Intercolonial. The St. John Valley railway is tc be extended to meet the Transcontinental traffic and bring it across by the short way into St. John and it is not to go around by the Intercolonial. If it were not to do that it would not be built. But we have an elevator to receive that traffic and we are charaging it up to the poor, overburdened Intercolonial railway which has everything charged to it when we cannot find some other account to charge to.

What does the minister
intend doing with the section of the Transcontinental railway between Levis and Moncton? I have heard that there is a great deal of congestion on the Intercolonial railway. Does he intend carrying the traffic that reaches Quebec, and that is to be sent down to Halifax and St. John, over the Intercolonial railway and not utilize that section of the Transcontinental railway?

The hon. member knows the position in which we have been during the past winter. The equipment on the Intercolonial was all the equipment we had, and that equipment was run over the Intercolonial and part over the Levis-Moncton branch, -and quite a lot of freight went over that branch at times during the winter. Until we can get more equipment for the Transcontinental it will be hard foT us to do more than we have been doing. We [DOT]have ordered a large -amount of equipment and we will operate the two systems to the best advantage. The branch from Levis to Moncton is a good road, and after next fall we will use it almost entirely for the St. John traffic, because we go in by McGivn-ey junction and on down to St. John. I hope that the elevator which we will have at St. John next year will help us out very materially.
You are not going to carry any grain beyond Quebec next summer?

Not likely, because when it gets to Quebec it is at an ocean port, and it would only be adding so much to the freight to carry it on to St. John or Halifax. Of course, there are transports being sent to Canadian ports by the Admiralty, and some of them may be ordered to St. John or Halifax even during the summer months, and the Admiralty may order us to take grain, or hay, or ammunition to those ports. In that case, we will carry out their instructions, but it is not natural to carry freight past Quebec or Montreal during the summer months.
What kind of a passenger service is given between Levis and Moncton on the Transcontinental?
The road is in operation and a tri-weekly passenger service is given.
Is there a regular freight service?
Freight is also carried.
Will the service be improved during the coming summer?

We are at present able to keep up the freight -and passenger service fairly well and we will keep it up during the summer. Now that navigation has opened on the St. Lawrence, with the equipment we have we do not anticipate much trouble along the road.

Has the minister been giving serious consideration- to the ques-

t-ion of the elevator capacity for storage purposes at the citj* of Quebec? If the Transcontinental is to be used to any extent, I suppose the Government will wish to get as much grain as possible to Quebec in the fall for shipment out in- the spring.
We have a storage capacity of 1,500,000 bushels.
Has the Government that storage?
That is -under the Harbour Commission.
It has no connection with the Government railway system?
No.

Has the Government
thought of developing elevator facilities' at the city of Quebec to handle the traffic coming over the Transcontinental from the West?

We have been thinking over that matter as well as elevator capacity at other points along the line, but we have not decided to do anything during the present year. We intend to see how we can get along with the capacity that we have during the coming season, and having the other two ports besides Montreal -and Quebec to take the grain- to, with this elevator that we are getting -at St. John, I anticipate we shall be able to handle a large quantity of grain. We did not provide for any more elevator capacity this year for the reason that we thought the grain would be going through pretty fast and that we would get along without much storage.
When the minister gets next year the elevator capacity that he speaks about -at St. John, does he expect that the connection that has been under discussion by the St. John v-alley will be completed?

The members of the .New
Brunswick Government told me that they expected to have that completed and ready for operation by the 1st of December, but in order to be sure, they asked that the date be filled in-I think it is February 1. That is the understanding that I have with them.

If you have the elevator
ready, you can reach it over the Intercolonial.

Just the same; it is only a
question of so many miles further.

During the past winter
the department put into force between Winnipeg and Montreal or Quebec a rate that was recognized as a very reasonable one, and one which competed with water traffic, but they did not put in a rate from Quebec or Montreal to St. John. They are going to build an elevator, at St. John, but unless they put in a rate to St. John that will correspond with the rate that they put into force during the past winter from Winnipeg to Quebec or Montreal, they might as well not build that ,elevator. It will be of no use because last winter's rate was so adjusted that it simply made it possible to use the storage capacity at Montreal and Quebec without any advantage to the shipper and did not make it possible to use the accommodation at St. John, because there was no rate reduction that would enable that to be done. I am asking the minister if, in view of the proposed construction of this elevator at St. John, it is to be the policy of the department that a through rate to the port of St. John will be given at a corresponding charge per mile to that given last winter from Winnipeg to Quebec.

That rate from Winnipeg to Quebec proved to be quite an advantage. There was an enormous quantity of grain in the West last year, and pressure was put on the Minister of Railways to see if he could do anything to relieve the congestion. He had only a small equipment-just what he could take from the Intercolonial. At Montreal and Quebec there was quite a large storage capacity that was not being filled. If the Canadian Pacific Railway took the grain through, they would take it right to St. John, because they had an elevator there, and if the Grand Trunk took it through, they would take it to their elevators at Portland. We had no elevators at St. John and there was not much chance of the Transcontinental taking grain to St. John.

I do not wish to revive
that argument. All I am asking is, what is the policy for the future?

I want to show the hon.
member that the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) said: as an experiment we will take this grain to Montreal at the same rate as the summer rate of last year, that is 6 cents, and fill those elevators. That, of course, must have been a great advantage during the winter.
227J

It was a certain amount
of advantage.

If there had been elevator
capacity at Fort William, the grain would have gone there and the shippers would have had to pay the same storage rates as they would at Montreal, so the storage question was exactly the same.

That is right.
Mr.* REID: As to the question of what is to be done next year; the hon. member knows that through rates are always made between Winnipeg, or the West, and ocean ports. That matter will he taken up by the minister and his general freight agent,, and a conclusion will be reached, as to a. through rate between' Winnipeg and St-John and Halifax. This grain that went, through last fall all went to Montreal and' Quebec, except a small quantity.

I said a little while ago that I should be glad to see elevator capacity provided at St. John, and wished the minister to go as far as he likes in establishing that capacity. But, of course, that is all contingent on the winter railway rate to St. John being on a basis that will enable the grain to be brought forward in winter. I made a little calculation some time ago on- this subject, and I find that the winter rate from Winnipeg to' Quebec was 12 cents for 1,352 miles. From Quebec to St. John, by the present route-that is by Transcontihental to Moncton and thence by Intercolonial to St. John-is 541 miles. At thfe same rate per mile as was charged from Winnipeg to Quebec, the rate would be 4i cents, or a total rate from Winnipeg to St. John of 16J cents. But the rate actually charged from Winnipeg to St. John this winter, whether by the Canadian Pacific railway through Montreal or by Transcontinental by Montreal or Quebec, was 201 cents. That just made the difference between a rate that would bring traffic and a rate that would stop traffic.
Did I understand the hon. member to say that grain from Winnipeg to St. John either by the Canadian Pacific or the Transcontinental would be 201 cents?

Yes. The rate from Quebec or Montreal to St. John was so much higher per mile than the rate from Winnipeg to Montreal, that it balanced up and made the through rate just the same as that of the Canadian Pacific. If that policy is continued next year, there is very little object in building the elevator, or certainly a

very small elevator would. answer the purpose. But my view is that the purpose of the building of the Transcontinental was to enable a winter movement of grain to the Atlantic ports to be carried on. What has been done this winter goes to prove that this is practicable; and it is in view of that that I am urging the construction of the elevator at St. John and that next winter a freight rate to St. John 'be charged that will be as good on a mileage 'basis as that given this winter from Winnipeg to Quebec. If that is not done, there is no great advantage in establishing any large elevator accommodation at St. John. The Quebec Board of Trade has gone1 into this matter very thoroughly, and amongst the figures they have given in their report is the statement that grain is now hauled from Goderich, a lake port, to Halifax, a distance of 1,231 miles, at 6 1-10 cents per bushel. That seems to be a low rate. If credence is given to their statement, then it is manifest that the through rate given on the Transcontinental is not phenomenally low, but one at which the railway ought to do business. If it was able to do business between Winnipeg and Quebec, it surely was able to do business between Winnipeg and St. John.
I wish to add a word to what the acting minister (Mr. Reid) said with regard to the storage at Quebec. While St. John is an open port all the year around, and while there is therefore some argument for there being only transfer accommodation there, Quebec is a sealed port for a part of the year. And it is beyond any question that Quebec has tremendous advantages in the summer time over any other possible port of Canada. And, as it is a substantially shorter distance from the prairies to Quebec by the Transcontinental than by any other present railroad route to Montreal, there is every reason why there should be ample storage accommodation at Quebec. So, while we desire the advantage of the open port at St. John during the whole of the winter, at the same time we shall always be very glad to save the cost of haul from Levis to St. John by taking advantage of the storage at Quebec, so that the grain may have to carry the least possible charge in getting to market. That is the whole purpose of this discussion, and of all this railroad building and elevator building-it is to cut down the cost of transport and handling between the producer and the consumer. With present world conditions, with the world crop increasing as it has been increasing, there is 
no doubt that from year to year it becomes more and more, necessary, if our production is to increase by reason of the prosperity of our people, that the cost of transport and handling and the profits received between the producer and consumer, must be systematically cut down by every means possible. That is the main duty and responsibility of the department of the Government over which my hon. friend presides, and that will be arrived at by the use of the Transcontinental and by the isubsidary accommodation of ample elevators at St. John and Quebec.

The intention of the Government in reducing all rail rates over the National Transcontinental railway to 6 cents a bushel to Montreal and Quebec for export no doubt was good. But notwithstanding all that the minister has said since his Estimates have been up, he has not convinced me-and I do not believe that there is any man in the trade that has been convinced-that it worked out to be of any particular advantage either to the shipper or to the farmer. I will tell th-: minister why. The great trouble last year was to get grain on wheels. Grain on wheels right through the season was worth a premium running from 3J cents to as high as 8 cents a bushel over the May price; consequently the exporters could see a good deal'better profit in buying the May option and waiting for the opening of navigation. The minister has laid a good deal of stress on the advantage which this arrangement gave and the amount of grain that was carried to Quebec and Montreal for export. Last year when navigation closed in the fall there was a considerable amount of grain in the elevators at Montreal. I have not the figures before me, but we do know from a statement brought down here that some of the New Zealand wheat put there last summer was still in the elevators at Montreal in the month of March. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Edmonton, this special rate of 6 cents a bushel was good only going to Montreal or Quebec for export. If the grain was re-consigned from Montreal or Quebec to St. John or Halifax for export, the shippers had to go back to the regular rate enforced by the Canadian Pacific, Canadian Northern and Grand Trunk Railway Companies-and that rate was 23.3 cents per hundred pounds. Notwithstanding the enormous amount of grain that the minister claims was carried by the National Transcontinental, my statement is correct that this rate was of practically no value. A good deal of grain was carried, but I think we got practically the
full rate for it. It was probably more profitable to the country and to the railroad not to carry it at the cheap rate, but very little grain was carried on that cheap rate. A return brought down in the House told us, I think, that altogether there were 80 cars to one point and twenty to the other- something like that, more or less. I have here the statistics of the wheat in Canada, issued on April 3 by the Department of Trade and Commerce. It shows that the total quantity of wheat in the elevator at Quebec on that date was 99,000 bushels. No ships had come up to Quebec at that time, so that this was wheat which had been carried there during the winter; possibly some of the grain had been left over in the fall when navigation closed. There were 42,917 bushels of oats there and 5,000 bushels of barley. The total quantity of grain in the elevator in the city of Quebec on April 3 was 148,920 bushels. Remember that the elevator at the city of Quebec has a capacity of a million and a,half bushels; so that you can put a good deal of grain there yet before you require other elevators. The elevators at Montreal have a capacity of 15,000,000 bushels. How much grain do you think there was in Montreal on the third of April? The total quantity of all grain 9 p.m. in Montreal on that date was just a little over a million and a half bushels. These are official statements published by the Department of Trade and Commerce, I imagine they must be correct. There is some justification for the minister's statement that we require more storage capacity at West St. John, because we find that on that date there were at West St. John a total of 950,093 bushels of grain, of which 730,516 bushels were wheat. At Halifax on that date there were 36,685 bushels of grain. So we could carry a good deal of grain down to those ports before we should need to start building elevators. Instead of listening to the demands of local people who are anxious to see construction going on in their cities; instead of running the risk of repeating the mistake that was made at Calgary, where we put up a big elevator that is practically of no use as a transfer elevator because it is located out of the running belt of grain, it would be well for the department to think out some plan of establishing elevators where they are most needed and where they will earn some money. Elevators with a capacity of 15,000,000 bushels in which only a million and a half

bushels are stored are not earning very much money for the shareholders, the Government. There is a great demand upon the Government for money for the different railroads. I imagine they need money, but I do not think they need it so much for the extension of their lines as they do for rolling stock. It seems to me that if the Government were to figure on a plan of owning, say, 10,000 freight cars and of leasing them at reasonable rates to the railroads during the grain carrying season, that would be of more advantage to the western farmer just now than elevator capacity. He does not want elevator capacity unless he can get the grain out of the elevator. We know from the experience of the past winter that there are sections in the West where very little grain has yet been moved. Take the Gilbert Plains district; I am told that many farmers there have not been able to ship a carload. What this country requires is more freight cars and more power. That is what the railroads need, not more miles of railway or more elevators. I submit this to the consideration of the minister, without condemning too strongly this policy of greater elevator capacity. I think that there is an indication at West St. John that we need it. But certainly we must get more grain down to Montreal and Quebec before we start talking of building greater elevator capacity.

With all due respect to the hon. minister, we all have our own opinions as to the best way to improve this transportation system. The hon. member does not think it is good policy to have so many elevators where water navigation commences. My own opinion has always been that that is where we do require storage. Fort William and Port Arthur form the first water port, and surely we should there have as large storage capacity as possible. My own opinion is that if a farmer can load his grain in the winter on the car and get it right through to Quebec or Montreal at the same rate as it would cost for summer transportation through Port Arthur or Fort William, and have his grain stored at the seaboard instead of at Port Arthur, he would save the elevator charges on the grain at Fort Arthur. I think we should have large storage capacity at Port Arthur or at the head of the lakes, and also at Montreal, St. John and Halifax. As to the quantity of grain in Quebec and Montreal, the manager of the railways told me that they put one and a half million bushels of grain into the elevators at Quebec, and

between Quebec and Montreal they had eight million bushels from the West over the National Transcontinental railway. I asked Mr. Hayes, the general freight agent, and those were the figures he gave me. What became of it after that I am not in a position to say, and we could not ascertain until after navigation opened. For instance, we may have put five million or six million bushels into 'the elevators at Montreal. That may have gone on by the Canadian Pacific railway; the parties who owned the grain may have had it re-shipped to Portland over the Grand Trunk railroad, ot to St. John over the Canadian Pacific railroad. The hon. member states that there would be no advantage to the western farmer providing it had been reshipped from Montreal. My understanding of it is that if you shipped last winter over the Canadian Pacific railroad or the Canadian Northern railroad, or the Grand Trunk under the old through rates, the winter rate was, say, 6 cents from Winnipeg to Fort [DOT] William. Then I think it was 12 cents to Montreal, and then a certain amount, which I do not know, from Montreal to Portland over the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Pacific railroad rate from Montreal to St. John being the same. Taking the figures,
6 cents to Fort William and 12 cents to Montreal, and whatever the other rate was Montreal to Portland or St. John, the through rate from Winnipeg to Portland or St. John would be 18 cents plus the rate Montreal to the winter port. The advantage which the farmer in the West got was that he paid 6 cents from Winnipeg to Armstrong and 6 'cents to Montreal. If it was then shipped on to Portland or St. John he paid the pro rata rate from Montreal to Portland or St. John that through grain pays, and he thus had the advantage of the 6-oent rate against the 12-cent rate between Armstrong and Montreal, or between Fort William and Montreal. The farmers in the West, if they got the advantage of the 6-cent rate, paid only 12 cents a bushel from Winnipeg to Montreal and Quebec, as .against 18 cents if consigned to Montreal during the winter on the Canadian Pacific railroad. On our rate it was 6 cents to Armstrong and 6 cents to Montreal, or 12 cents against the rate I have stated. That is the advantage it was to the shipper.

There is not much difference between the minister's view and mine on the storage capacity at the head o' the

Great Lakes. He will admit that we have immense storage capacity there now. It has been fairly well filled this year, but there has always been room for a little more. But to come back to the rate, I have told the minister how much grain there was, according to the statistics furnished by the Department of Trade and Commerce, in Montreal and in Quebec, on the 3rd of April. The minister himself gave an answer from his own department on the 1st of March, according to Hansard, giving the number of cars shipped on that rate from Armstrong to Montreal, at 20 cars and from Armstrong to Montreal and 80 cars to Quebec. That clears up that matter from the statistics and as furnished in the minister's own answer. Probably the minister is right as to the rate from Winnipeg to Fort William, but that is not the way to figure on grain. The rate from Brandon to Fort William or Armstrong is 14 cents a hundred pounds. Tariff C G 18 gives the rate as 6 cents from Armstrong to Montreal or Quebec for export. Then there is a notation re consigning:
If grain is loaded out for export by Halifax, N.S., St. John, N.B., Portland, Maine, or Boston, Mass., through rates from Armstrong, Ont., will be applied in accordance with Transcontinental railway tariff, No. (C.G. 12 and C.G. 13) and supplements thereof.
Here is C G 13, giving the rates from Armstrong to St. John and Halifay. That rate is 23.3 per 100 pounds on grain and grain products. Then the rate to Portland, Maine, is the same, 23.3 (No. 3-G 12). The minister can settle that question with his traffic department.

I was not present when the minister answered an inquiry which I made a few days ago, but I have had an opportunity of seeing the telegram which he read to the House, and I find that it is neither full nor frank, and', besides, is misleading. The garden plot at Antigonish station was constructed I think last year, and although as rich alluvial soil can be got in and around Antigonish as is to be had in' any part of the Maritime Provinces, they actually went to Malagash station, between 100 and 150 miles distant, to get loam to make that plot. According tb the telegram, after they had unloaded four cars, it was found that two cars were sufficient, and they sent the balance of the stuff down to Mulgrave. Here is where the information is misleading: My information is that after the plot was completed the yard was so overcrowded that businessmen protested because of the obstruction to traffic, and that, consequently, they reduced it by about half. What I want to find out is what it cost to make the reduction. What became of the loam that was taken from Malagash when there was excellent soil right on the spot? Was it given to some friend to 'be taken away at his own expense,. or was it given to him at a price? Did he cart it away free of charge or was the carting paid for? It is notorious that teams carried that stuff through the town. I want to find out from the minister where it went, and what the arrangement was, whether this man was paid for trucking that stuff from the station and through the town, and, if so, how much he was paid. Therefore I would like the minister to supplement the information given in that telegram. I received a copy of it from his secretary and sent a reply suggesting that this information should be given. Perhaps the minister can give it now.

I told my secretary to see
that the information was given to the hon. member. It does seem strange that they should go 100 miles away for loam, but I am a farmer myself, and I know that sometimes it is good policy to have a change of soil; if you took some soil from Ontario and mix it with Nova Scotia soil, you might have better crops.
We have the best of crops in Antigonish.

I know that some farmers in Ontario get soil from Nova Scotia, and very good stuff it is. I get carload after carload of it, and I think that next time I will urge the manager to send to Ontario for soil and have it mixed) with the Nova Scotia soil. I will be very glad to get the information which the hon. member wants. He can see that I did my best to get it, but if they have not furnished it in full, I will get it at the earliest possible moment.

I thank the minister for the efforts he has made to secure the information. But the case referred to is on a par with a good deal of the work that these highly trained specialists, who have been hired, borrowed, or imported from the Canadian Pacific railway and other railroads, have been doing on the Intercolonial railway. Just fancy going 100 or 150 miles to get loam for a place like Antigonish where there is alluvial -soil of the richest kind. The minister has treated the matter

in a rather joking vein, and I do not wonder at it. The thing is ridiculous. It is a small matter, and I apologize for bringing it up, but it is a sample of the way in which those connected with the Intercolonial railway do things.

We have had a good deal of argument about the transportation of wheat last winter at the low rate. I understood very distinctly from the minister that that rate was for the purpose of filling the elevators, of utilizing the storage capacity of the elevators at Montreal and Quebec.
That is right.

But by the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce, that statement is not borne out, so< far as the Quebec elevator is concerned. We will assume that the grain delivered at the Montreal elevator was passed' on to Portland or St. John by the other road, but, so far as the Quebec elevator is concerned, there was no such opportunity. Grain was certainly not forwarded from Quebec to St. John or from Halifax, because the Halifax elevator was not filled; therefore it could not have been put into the Quebec elevator. As long as there was vacant space in Quebec, and there was grain in the West to bring forward, the Transcontinental railway was not fulfilling its purpose, nor was the rate being utilized.

All I can say is that I had the assurance of our general freight agent that that quantity of grain was put into the Quebec elevator and came over the Transcontinental railway during the past winter. The statement submitted by the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) is headed: " The total quantity in store on March 24, 1916." Whether or not the grain came after that date, or whether it went in and was shipped on again, is a question regarding which I have not information at present. I shall get the general freight agent to give me in writing a statement of the quantity of grain which went in, and I will give the hon. member for Edmonton the information. I will either show him that 1,500,000 bushels-it might have been a little more or less-went from Quebec, or I will stand up here and admit that I was wrong. But I got that information from him only ten days ago in this very building, and of course I must adhere to it. I will be able tto give my hon. friend fuller information, I hope, within the next 48 hours. I will have the exact figures for Montreal and Quebec and the dates on which the grain

was put in. From the close of navigation up to a few days ago, eight million bushels went into the Montreal and Quebec elevators.

The hon. member for
Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) suggested that if this railroad was to meet the purposes for which it was intended, there would have to be more rolling stock provided. I am not familiar with the workings of the Department of Railways, but, from what the minister has said during the discussions in the House, it would seem to me that it is a fact, that there is not sufficient rolling stock in the hands of the Government to handle a large amount of traffic over the Transcontinental. Is it proposed by the department to take measures to increase that rolling stock adequately so as to be able to bring forward a large quantity of grain during the winter months, .and to what extent?
I am going to award contracts for cars within the next three or four weeks; probably $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 worth will be ordered1.
Is there anything for that in the Estimates?

We have a part of the money in the Estimates and we have our Intercolonial surplus. The hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) is right; if we had 10,000 cars and 200 engines it would be a great advantage but 10,000 cars would cost $10,000,000 or $12,000,000. These iron freight cars cost $1,200 or $1,400 each. They used [DOT]to cost about $1,100 but they are now . worth, I expect, $200 or $300 more. We cannot buy $10,000,000 or $12,000,000 worth of care j.ust now. You require power, vans and a lot of equipment. We will get these things as fast as we can. With reference to the rate question, as I stated during a previous discussion, we only started in last year as an experiment with this Transcontinental railway, we started in without equipment, without organization and just to get a little experience, we put on this 6-oent rate and handled 8,000,000 bushels of grain with such equipment as we had divided between the two roads-. We expect to have sufficient equipment to enable us to handle a very large quantity of grain next winter. With good organization and extra equipment we will be of great service to the West next year.

With the acquisition of the Forget road, and the opening of a

*winter port at St. Catharine's bay, will not the conditions be entirely changed at St. John and Halifax?
There ie work for all our winter ports.
Where is Ste. Catherine's bay?

Across the Saguenay river from Tadousac there is a large bay and a splendid harbour. This road was first intended to go to Ste. Catherine's bay. Murray bay is within 30 or 40 miles of Ste. Catherine's bay.
Will the port at Ste. Catherine's bay be open in the winter?
Yes, they tell me that it is open nearly all winter.
Is that an official report?

I understand that to be so,
but I will see if there is any official report.

Our friends from the
West and from the Maritime Provinces who take an interest in this grain question might very well be informed in regard to this because conditions may be entirely changed. If we can regard Ste. Catherine's bay as the open winter port of the St. Lawrence the other ports in the Maritime Provinces may look very small. There is no rolling stock at all on the Quebec and Saguenay railway at the present time?

I do not know that there is, but there is on some other part of the road. The hon. gentleman talks about the Quebec and Saguenay railway! He knows to-day that from Quebec to Saguenay there were the electric and steamboat services which are really part of the system.
The electric road running between Quebec and Ste. Anne de Beaupre does a very large business in carrying pilgrims to the shrine at Ste Anne, but beyond that I do not think there is much business.

Then there will be pilgrimages to St. Catherine's bay. I would like to divert the Minister's attention from what must be an unpleasant situation to one which will give him more joy. I was told recently by a gentleman who lives in Chipman that every day there are long trains of cars full of freight passing over the Transcontinental railway that it is no uncommon thing to see one locomotive hauling a train half a mile long over this level
road bed. I want to ask the minister if he has any report with regard to the traffic which is being carried on that line and where that traffic originates?

I have not that information but the hon. gentleman knows that both of these roads belong now to the Government and they will be operated by the Government. It is only natural that we should operate them in the very best way possible for the Government. If we could haul 50 cars between Levis and St. John over the Transcontinental railway we would not start a train over the Intercolonial with 25 or 30 cars if that was all we could take.
That shows the advantage of the Transcontinental railway grades.

I know, but at the same time it has cost us a great many millions to build that road. I do not want to go into a discussion of the Transcontinental railway system to-night. We have done it very often before, and I do not think there is anything to be gained by it. That road was built to run in opposition to the Intercolonial. Now that we own it, we intend to operate the two roads as a business proposition, and if we have a lot of cars at LAvis to take to St. John or Moncton, or, if you wish, to Halifax, we are going to take them with engines that will draw all the cars possible, and operate the roads in the best possible manner.

The minister says that we "own" it. That affords a text for some quite lengthy remarks. When did we secure the ownership of it? Some time ago I asked the right hon. Prime Minister if any permanent arrangement had been made for the Government operation of the Transcontinental railway, and he said: No permanent arrangement could be made except by legislation and the action of Parliament. No such legislation has yet been introduced. Therefore, I would like to know why the minister, in contradistinction to the statement of the Prime Minister, says that we own the Transcontinental.

I will tell the hon. gentleman why I think we own it. I was under the impression that according to the Act passed the Government had built that portion of the road between Winnipeg and Moncton and owned it, and that we were to lease it to the Grand Trunk Pacific. So, I say we own it, and I think I am not mistaken in that. Am I not right in the statement that we were to build, own and lease

it for a certain number of years, and that the Grand Trunk were to pay interest upon it? That is the reason I say that we own it.
The minister said that it was built as a road which was to be run in competition with the Intercolonial railway?
Certainly.
But the minister says now that we own it, as if something had taken place which had taken away the right of the Grand Trunk Pacific to operate it and placed the ownership in the Crown.

The hon. gentleman is drawing a pretty fine distinction. I did say that it was .built to be run in competition with the Intercolonial railway. The original proposition was that the Government should build, own and lease it to the Grand Trunk Pacific.
But did not the minister say now that we owned it, as if there had been some change in the ownership? ,

There is no change in the ownership. We are operating it, if you wish to draw that fine distinction. However, we are operating it and we will no doubt do so to the advantage of the public. But this afternoon I noticed that the hon. gentleman was criticising the Government and asking why they should not take over the Grand Trunk Pacific at once and operate it. He found fault because we would not take over and operate the whole line between Winnipeg and the Pacific coast. Now he is finding fault beoause we did take over t'he Transcontinental.
Is the minister referring to me?
Yes.
When did I .so argue?
I understood that to-day my hon. friend's argument was that we should take over these roads beoause they were bankrupt; that giving money to them was not in the public interest.

What I said was that, as these companies are now coming to the Government and are saying in effect: We are bankrupt; we cannot carry on the operation of these roads any ionger, unless you assist us, and as the Government, according to the .statements of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Public Works are looking forward to the nationalization of the railways of Canada, they ought now, as a condition of giving this assistance,
[Mr. J. D. Reid.l
to stipulate for a maximum price at which the country would have in the future the right to take over the roads. In other words, this country should not help them over this period of adversity and then put them in a position, when the time of prosperity comes, to demand what they please for the roads, including prospective profits, which might amount to a very large sum.
At all events, the discussion to-day would surely convince the hon. member that the Grand Trunk Pacific is not in a position to operate this road between Winnipeg and Montreal.
Not immediately.

And that is the reason why the Government is operating it. We believe that next session, when we have a report as to the whole railway situation, there can be a reorganization of the railway system of Canada that will be a great advantage to every one concerned. As the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance stated to-day, something must be done. It will be only six or eight months until we meet again, and .then we shall be in a position to go thoroughly into the whole railway system and see what is best to be done under the circumstances in the interest of the public.
Are you going to have a fall session?
That may be necessary.

As the minister has been
discussing the matter of providing more equipment during the coming summer for the operation of the Transcontinental and the Intercolonial railway, I want again to protest as strongly as I can to the minister againstr the Government robbing the Intercolonial of its rolling stock, and curtailing the freight and passenger service of the Maritime Provinces over the Intercolonial, and in this way destroying the Intercolonial for the benefit of the Transcontinental. That is what happened last winter. As I pointed out to the minister the other evening, the Intercolonial was made simply a local road in so far as through traffic was concerned. Traffic was held up; passenger trains running from Montreal to Halifax were delayed five, six or ten hours simply because the rolling stock of the Intercolonial was taken away and placed on the Transcontinental for the purpose of keeping that road in operation. That was inequitable and

unfair to the people of the Maritime Provinces for whose service the Intercolonial railway was really built. My hon. friend said that he proposed to buy three or four million dollars' woTth of rolling stock apparently for the Transcontinental and the Intercolonial, and he stated that there was not enough in the Estimates, hut that he was going to take the surplus from the Intercolonial and put it into rolling stock.

I did not say that; I said
that some was going to be taken from the surplus of the Intercolonial and that that would be put on the Government railway system. I do not think the hon. member will object to rolling stock being run through from Levis to Moncton. We will operate the stock on both roads. In addition to that surplus an amount has been placed in the Estimates for the Transcontinental. I said we were going to take the money from both the surplus and the Estimates, but it has alfvays been the policy to use any surplus there may he on the Intercolonial for purchasing rolling stock for the Intercolonial. The hon. member has argued before that it was not right to take any part of the Intercolonial equipment last year. We could not get any equipment from any otheT railway; the Grand Trunk Pacific was to have some rolling stock for the Transcontinenal, but we did not get a car, and if we had not used a small portion of the Intercolonial rolling stock for the Transcontinental, we could not have operated it at all. I do not think the hon. member will say that we should have closed up the Transcontinental and not operated it at all between Winnipeg and Moncton during last winter. There were settlements along the line, and it was necessary to have some passenger traffic. There had to be cars and engines for that and supplies had also to be taken in and out. There was also this grain in the West that had to be carried out. Some people along the Intercolonial were inconvenienced, but there would have been much more hardship if we had had to close up the Transcontinental. We did our best to get what equipment we could, but we did not get it in time.
Mr. iCOFP: I do not intend to argue at length in regard to the conditions of last winter, because it is past and gone. Things are better now; the snow has disappeared, and the freight is going through much more rapidly. I rose, however, to enter my protest on behalf of the people of the Maritime Provinces in the future. My hon. friend says he would not think I would say that we should not operate the Transcontinental. I am not in a position to say that we should operate the Transcontinental or not. It is only a few years ago that those settlements spoken of by the acting minister, along the Transcontinental, have had railway accommodation. The people of the Maritime Provinces have had the Intercolonial ever since Confederation, and I contend1 that the minister had no right to rob the Intercolonial and sacrifice the rights of the people who are served by that railway for the benefit of the people who live along the Transcontinental. I want to put myself on record as protesting in the strongest manner possible that during the coming summer and the coming winter the Intercolonial should have proper rolling stock as it has had in the past and not have it depleted, as it was during the past winter, for the benefit of the Transcontinental. Whatever surplus has been laid aside from the Intercolonial should be expended on the betterment of that railway, both in roadbed and equipment, in order to give that railway its proper status as the railway which has served the people of the Maritime Provinces since Confederation, and I say that its interests should not be sacrified to those of- any other great transcontinental railway.

What the minister has
said in regard to the provision of rolling stock is rather of the character that he is going to strain a point in order to get some rolling stock for the Transcontinental. The Transcontinental has cost the country something like $200,000,000 to build, and that capital expenditure is of no value unless there is rolling stock to handle the business over the road. There was business this year to be handled if we had had the rolling stock. Unfortunately we may not have as much business next year because we have not been able to handle the business this year.
The question should be approached, not in any parsimonious spirit, but in the spirit of meeting the conditions of traffic as they exist and may be expected to exist some time in the near future. Of last season's crop, something like sixty or seventy million bushels found its outlet by way of Buffalo. Of this year's crop 125,000,000 bushels remain in the West,, still to come forward; and if it comes forward at all, it will come by the lakes, and the larger part of that

crop will find its way out by Buffalo. We are producing the crop and it is the United Kingdom that needs it; and we have built railroads at enormous cost to do this very traffic; yet we allowed the traffic to pass away from us both last year and this year. We are continually talking of not having business for our railroads, but this year we not only have business but an enormous amount of business which has gone away from us simply because we were not prepared to handle it. What I urge is that means be taken to utilize the transportation facilities of the Transcontinental railway by ample elevator capacity at the winter port of St. John and at the summer port of Quebec, and by ample rolling stock to bring the crop forward all the year around so that we shall not be in the position in the future of carrying on the production and other people doing the business.
It has been generally assumed that because the grain has come forward by the lakes up to the present time, it must always come forward by the lakes. There is no ground for that supposition. When the Erie canal was built all grain from the West went by the Erie canal; but to-day the amount that goes by the Erie canal is little; the railways having displaced the water transportation to a tremendous degree. The Great Lakes, of course, are on a larger scale than lake Ontario or the St. Lawrence, or our canals; but the position of the Transcontinental from Winnipeg to Quebec is one of vast advantage. I do not see that there is any reason why the conditions which prevailed in regard to water traffic on lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence canals, in which the traffic has practically been driven off the lake, should not be repeated as between the Transcontinental and Canadian Northern on one hand and the navigation of the Groat Lakes on the other. Of course, having built the railroads, we must equip them with rolling stock and other facilities. But let us not sit down and complain that we have not the business to do when the city of Buffalo and the American business of transportation on the Great Lakes is being built up out of the business that we create.

I wish to refer to a matter not relevant to that which has been discussed, but which, I understand, comes within the minister's announcement of *willingness to discuss any matter relating to has department. The question is that of deep water facilities at Newcastle, N.B. A

survey was made and a proposition to extend the wharf. Nothing further has been done. When I was at home I found some of my constituents making inquiry about the matter, and I promised to 'have it brought to the attention of the minister.
I will place on Hansard or give to the hon. gentleman, when we are discussing some other railway item, a full explanation of that matter.

Now that the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has shown that what we require is more rolling stock for the railway, which is the idea that I have urged, I wonder if we could not go a little further and let that Hudson bay scheme lie over for a year or two, and put the money into ships to carry grain from Atlantic ports to Liverpool. It is of little use to bring grain to deep water if you have not ships to carry it to the other side. Would not the minister think it well to take some of this money that some of us think is being wasted in the Hudson bay scheme and put it into ships?

Personally, I have strong opinions on the question of ships. To buy new ships is impossible at the present time
there are none for sale. And if you start to build a new ship now you will not get it for a year.

This is a good
time to commence.

Yes, but you have to consider that the cost of a ship in normal times is about $50 a ton, while now it is $120 per ton. A vessel of 10,000 tons would cost you in normal times $500,000, but today the cost would be $1,200,000, and you would not have the use of it for a year. If the war was going to last two or three years it would be a good idea to order ships and have tnem for the year's operations. Under present conditions, ii you were to pay $1,200,000 to have delivered to you in a year's time a vessel which, under ordinary conditions, would cost $500,uuO, the investment mignt not be a very good one. I am strongly in favour of building vessels in our own country; but whether we build them in our own country or not you cannot get them at less, roughly speaking, than $120 a ton. These are tne figures I have had given to me in discussing this subject with shipbuilders. I have in mind the case of a man who has in course of construction a 10,000-ton vessel which he expects to be finished in July; and he tells

me that he can get just double his contract'' price for the vessel, but he could not get another, probably, for more than twice as much as the contract. These are things to be taken into consideration. My idea is that if we had normal conditions we ought a^ once to start shipbuilding in our own country. We are a growing country and we require vessels to take our own products from our own ocean terminals to foreign countries; and by doing that and connecting with our own railway service we caD greatly increase our trade.
We are facing these difficulties now, and in view of the conditions it is hard to tell what is really the best thing to be done. This consideration, together with the great expenditures for war, makes us hesitate to engage in such work as is suggested by the hon. member. The hon. member is absolutely right; we should have these vessels and run them in connection with our railways. But the hon. member is a business man, and he can see why we should hesitate to give an order for a vessel which in these times would cost $1,200,000 and in normal times $500,000.
Will not the prices be equally high for a period of five years after the war?

There is a difference of opinion on that. Some men say that they will be higher than they were in normal times, because so. many vessels are being destroyed. Others say that there will he a very large drop in the price for the reason that a large number of vessels are interned at the present time, and a very large number of vessels are being used by different nations for their own purposes of transport. These will all again come into the mercantile trade, and that will tend to bring freights down and reduce the cost of building vessels. I have seen no one yet who will make the statement that as soon as the war is over the cost of building vessels will keep up to what it is at the present time. I think the drop will be very considerable.

It is very satisfactory that the minister endorses that idea. If I understand him rightly, he claims that under normal conditions after the war we could build three ships for the price of one that we could build now. The extra expenses would be in the matter of labour and iron, I imagine?
Yes.
Would not the same principle apply to the Hudson Bay railway? Would it not be just as well to delay that work until after the war, when labour and iron will be cheaper?

No, because the Hudson Bay railway is under contract. Of course, we are holding it down; we are not doing nearly the amount of work we should do in normal times. We are holding it down as much as we can without rendering ourselves liable to the contractors for damages for shutting down the work.
That steamship that you are buying, is it by contract?

It is the Northumberland, that ran on that route a great many years. A company owned the Northumberland and the Empress, the former running between Summerside and Point du Chene and the latter between Pictou and Charlottetown.
Is the Government going to run that boat now between Point du Chene and Summerside?

The company have sold their boats. They sold the Empress to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and we bought the Northumberland. We are running the Northumberland between Point du Chene and Summerside, and we are running the car ferry between Pictou and Charlottetown.
All the communication, then, between the island and the mainland is being carried on by the Government?

Yes.
Canals-bridge between Iberville and St. John-revote of lapsed amount, $52,000.
